title: Nile Nexus at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Enhancing Fine-Grained Arabic Readability Assessment through Ordinal-Aware Transformer Ensembling and Decision Calibration
abstract: Readability assessment has played a vital role in education, yet most NLP work has focused on English and a few high-resource languages, leaving fine-grained Arabic readability comparatively unexplored. In the BAREC Shared Task 2026, we have addressed sentence-level classification into 19 ordinal readability levels under the Strict Track, fine-tuning four Arabic transformer encoders, MARBERT, CAMeLBERT MSA, AraELECTRA and AraBERTv2, on the official training split under multiple ordinal-aware losses: soft cross-entropy, squared Earth Mover's Distance, direct ordinal regression and a CORAL-style cumulative-threshold loss. A validation-only greedy ensemble of all resulting models, combined with a learned per-level threshold post-processing step, has raised performance from a best single-model QWK of 0.8341 to a final validation QWK of 0.8507. On the official Blind Test leaderboard, our system has achieved a QWK of 0.848, securing 3rd place in the Strict Track

title: Skywalker at BAREC Shared Task 2026: Multi-Expert PLM Fusion and QWK-Aware Ordinal Decoding
abstract: We present the system of Team Skywalker for the Sentence-level Strict track of the BAREC Shared Task 2026, which requires predicting one of 19 ordered Arabic readability levels for each sentence. Our system integrates complementary public Arabic pretrained language-model (PLM) experts fine-tuned with classification, regression, and ordinal objectives. Their continuous scores, confidence estimates, and rank-based features are combined using cross-fitted LightGBM meta-models. We further incorporate a cumulative ordinal branch that models level-boundary probabilities and a normalized-text branch that improves robustness to Arabic orthographic variation. Finally, a QWK-aware decoder maps the fused continuous score to one of the 19 readability levels using monotonic thresholds selected exclusively on the public validation set. We use only the official training data for supervision and the public validation labels for model selection. In addition to the final fusion system, we report single-PLM baselines and controlled ablations. The final configuration achieves a QWK of 86.30 on the public validation set and 84.20 on the CodaBench blind evaluation, ranking fourth among the submitted systems.

title: Soloeval at BAREC Shared Task 2026: QWK-Aligned Soft-Label Ordinal Classification with Auxiliary Surface Features for Arabic Readability Assessment
abstract: We describe Soloeval's submission to the Sentence-Level Open Track of the BAREC Shared Task 2026 on fine-grained Arabic readability assessment. Rather than treating the 19-level readability scale as a scalar regression target, we fine-tune pretrained Arabic BERT encoders (MARBERTv2 and CAMeLBERT-Mix) with a soft-label cross-entropy objective whose target distribution is a Gaussian centered on the gold level, chosen to more directly reflect the Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK) evaluation metric's quadratic distance penalty. We combine this with lightweight auxiliary surface features (sentence length, word count, diacritic density) and K-fold cross-validation. Our best single-model configuration, CAMeLBERT-Mix trained with F=3 folds, achieves a QWK of 80.6 on the BAREC 2026 blind test leaderboard for the Open track. We report our full hyperparameter search, discuss the gap between our dev- and test-set results, and outline what we would try next.

title: AraGenre 2026: A Hierarchical Definition-Guided Arabic Genre Classification Shared Task
abstract: AraGenre 2026 is a shared task on hierarchical, definition-guided Arabic genre classification under limited supervision and substantial distribution shift. Systems assign each text a broad label and a specific label using an inventory of six broad branches and 74 defined final genres. The final benchmark contains 27,972 source-derived Arabic segments, spanning Modern Standard Arabic, Classical Arabic, and dialectal material, while the released labelled examples are small and primarily synthetic. Final specific classes are absent from the released labelled data, but their English names and definitions are provided. The task received 46 registrations and 373 submissions, with 17 ranked final entries and 11 system description papers. Thaka achieved the highest official Hierarchical Macro F1 at 73.52, followed by HP at 71.69 and NAMAA-1 at 70.13. Broad classification was consistently stronger than specific classification. The documented systems frequently combine label semantics with multilingual retrieval, LLM judging, pseudo-labelling, reranking, or calibration. We clarify the resource-driven taxonomy and inherited gold labels, distinguish combined distribution shift from isolated unseen-label effects, and provide systematic validation of the final evaluation data.

title: HP at AraGenre 2026: LLM-Guided Pseudo-Labeling for Hierarchical Arabic Genre Classification with MARBERT
abstract: This paper presents the system submitted by team HP for the AraGenre 2026 Shared Task on Hierarchical Definition-Guided Arabic Genre Classification. To address the low-resource constraint of the provided dataset (140 labeled training samples), we propose a two-stage pipeline combining LLM-based pseudo-labeling with supervised fine-tuning. In the first stage, we evaluate several models under a 5-fold cross-validation framework, including Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite (0.9413), Qwen2.5 7B (0.7203), LLaMA 3.1 8B (0.6380), and a multilingual NLI model (0.3099). Based on these results, Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite is selected to generate pseudo-labels for the unlabeled test set using a definition-guided few-shot prompt. In the second stage, MARBERTv2 and ARBERTv2 are fine-tuned on approximately 28,000 pseudo-labeled samples. Our experiments show that MARBERTv2 achieves the best standalone score of 0.7169 Hierarchical Macro F1, outperforming both ARBERTv2 (0.7118) and a soft voting ensemble (0.7165), suggesting that Arabic-specialized pretraining of MARBERTv2 is more effective than model ensembling for this task.

title: ArGuard Shared Task: Harmful Content Detection in Arabic Memes and LLM Prompts
abstract: Harmful content appears in diverse forms, ranging from multimodal memes targeting protected groups to textual prompts designed to elicit unsafe responses from large language models. However, existing Arabic resources typically study these settings separately and often rely on coarse-grained labels. We introduce ArGuard, a shared task on harmful content detection in Arabic memes and LLM prompts. ArGuard consists of two tracks: Track A focuses on multimodal hate detection in Arabic memes, while Track B addresses harmful prompt detection for Arabic LLM safety evaluation. Overall, 58 teams registered for the shared task, 35 participated in the final evaluation phase, and 27 submitted system-description papers. Participating systems explored a range of approaches, including fine-tuning encoder- and decoder-based models such as AraBERT, Jais, and Qwen3-VL. The best-performing systems achieved macro-F1 scores of 0.823 on Subtask A1, 0.419 on Subtask A2, 0.984 on Subtask B1, and 0.790 on Subtask B2. These results highlight fine-grained meme classification (Subtask A2) as the most challenging setting, partly due to sparse labels and train-test distribution shifts. To facilitate further research on Arabic harmful-content detection, we release the task datasets and associated resources through the shared-task website.

title: dbilianos at ArGuard Shared Tasks: When Does Translation Help in Arabic Harmful Prompt Detection?
abstract: This paper describes the participation of the dbilianos team in the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task on harmful prompt detection for Arabic LLM safety evaluation. We participated in both subtasks: binary safe/unsafe classification (Task B1) and granular harm category classification (Task B2). Our approach systematically tested a central hypothesis: whether translating Arabic prompts into English improves classification performance. We experimented with multiple pipelines, including classical machine learning with TF-IDF features, zero-shot and few-shot prompting with DeepSeek-V4, and hybrid approaches. Our results reveal a divergence across subtasks. For binary classification, DeepSeek zero-shot on English translations achieved 0.89 macro-F1, securing 4th place in this subtask, and confirming that LLM-based prompting is highly effective for coarse-grained safety decisions. For granular classification, however, the best performance came from training a Support Vector Machine directly on original Arabic text using TF-IDF features, which achieved 0.61 macro-F1, placing the team 16th in this subtask. This outperformed our translation-based strategies, suggesting that fine-grained harm categorization is highly sensitive to linguistic and cultural nuance that is lost or distorted during translation. The translation hypothesis was only partially supported locally, and ultimately reversed on the final test set for both subtasks. We discuss implications for cross-lingual safety evaluation and highlight the limitations of translation-based pipelines for tasks requiring subtle intent interpretation.

title: NYUAD at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Embedding Models for Detecting Arabic Hateful Memes and Unsafe Prompts
abstract: The rapid growth of social media and generative AI has significantly increased the volume of Arabic textual content, memes, and user prompts shared across online platforms. While these media facilitate communication, creativity, and information exchange, they can also be exploited to disseminate hate speech, harmful content, and unsafe instructions. As a result, there is an increasing need for reliable automated methods to identify hateful Arabic memes and harmful (unsafe) prompts. This paper leverages pre-trained and fine-tuned multilingual embedding models to learn rich semantic representations from textual and visual content. The evaluation is conducted using a dataset of Arabic memes and prompts proposed in the ArabicNLP ArGuard 2026 challenge. The results underscore the capacity of large language model (LLM)-based embedding models to deliver superior performance. Developing robust detection systems is essential for improving content moderation and fostering a more secure and trustworthy online environment for Arabic-speaking users.

title: CalibGuard at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Threshold Calibration and Label-Space Constraints for Arabic Multimodal Hate Speech and Harmful Prompt Detection
abstract: This paper describes CalibGuard, our system for the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task on harmful content detection in Arabic memes and large language model prompts. We participate in all four subtasks: binary and fine-grained hateful meme classification (A1, A2) and binary and harm-domain prompt classification (B1, B2). For Task A, we extract frozen embeddings from three vision-text encoder pairs and train a joint two-headed classifier under 5-fold cross-validation with seed averaging. For Task B, we fine-tune AraBERTv02 with class-weighted cross-entropy. CalibGuard obtains 75.53\% macro-F1 on subtask A1, 36.53\% on A2, 65.38\% on B1 and 68.85\% on B2, ranking 11th, 3rd, 15th and 13th respectively. We further show that the B1 test split contains 49.3\% unsafe prompts against 79.8\% in training, and that this distribution shift accounts for a 29-point gap between our development and test scores, concentrated entirely in Modern Standard Arabic. Rethresholding to the test prior recovers 13.7 points without retraining. We additionally report two negative results: constrained decoding marginally reduces A2 performance, and restricting B2 training to unsafe prompts costs 5.7 points.

title: Axiom at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Unimodal Text Dominance for Arabic Hate Meme Detection
abstract: Detecting hate speech in social media memes requires disentangling complex cross-modal interactions, a challenge magnified in low-resource and morphologically rich languages like Arabic. We present Team Axiom's submission to the ArGuard 2026 Shared Task (Task A1) on binary hate meme classification. While conventional multimodal wisdom posits that text and visual features must be jointly fused, empirical evidence across non-English domains reveals that noisy visual backbones and cross-modal space misalignment frequently degrade language signals. We validate this hypothesis by fine-tuning a unimodal MARBERTv2 sequence classifier without external multimodal fusion. Our simple, well-regularized approach achieved a Macro-F1 of 0.770 and an accuracy of 0.818 on the official gold test set, securing 6th place on the global leaderboard and outperforming both the official AraBERTv2 baseline and our own complex multimodal fusion architectures.

title: SATLab at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Character N-Grams for Fine-Grained Categorization of Harmful LLM Prompts in Arabic
abstract: This paper presents SATLab's participation in the ArGuard 2026 shared sub-task on identifying seven types of harmful LLM prompts in Arabic. The proposed system is language-agnostic and requires no resources other than the training data provided in the shared task. It is based on character n-grams and a logistic regression classifier. Performance on the Test set (Macro-F1 = 0.736) was average, approximately 0.05 lower than that of the top teams (0.790) and approximately 0.05 higher than the baseline (0.687). Notably, this performance was substantially lower than those achieved in cross-validation and on the Development set. Several analyses aimed at understanding these discrepancies are reported. An analysis of the confusion matrix indicates that the ``Harm-to-other'' category poses the greatest problem, likely because it is partially compatible with all other categories except ``Adult-content''.

title: NAMAA at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Fusion, Vision--Language Model Adaptation, and In-Context Prompting for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
abstract: Multimodal hate speech detection requires interpreting how an image and its accompanying text jointly construct a target, stance, or derogatory implication. In Arabic memes, this relation is often shaped by locally recognizable public figures, political references, visual analogies, and indirect humor, making either modality insufficient on its own. We tackle this problem in Track A of ArGuard 2026, covering binary hateful meme detection (A1) and fine-grained multi-label classification (A2). Our experiments compare jointly trained dual encoders, parameter-efficient vision--language model (VLM) adaptation, and training-free prompting. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL, Llama 3.2 Vision, and Gemma 4 with QLoRA using task-specific binary and multi-label objectives. We also build CLIP--MARBERTv2 and SigLIP--AraBERT-Twitter cross-attention systems and evaluate frozen VLMs with zero-shot prompting and in-context learning. Qwen3-VL achieves our highest A1 score (0.7610), while SigLIP--AraBERT-Twitter leads A2 (0.3851), where label sparsity and multi-label prediction remain challenging.

title: StanceEval 2026: The Second Stance Detection Shared Task
abstract: StanceEval 2026 is the second edition of the StanceEval shared task series on stance detection in Arabic social media text. Stance detection aims to identify a writer's stance toward a given topic. Given a tweet and a target, participating systems must determine whether the writer's stance is Favor, Against, or None. This edition focuses on cross-target generalization across two distinct evaluation tracks: Track 1 evaluates thematically related cross-target transfer (testing on Women Driving, related to Women Empowerment in the training data), while Track 2 evaluates cross-domain transfer to completely unseen targets (E-Cars and Trimester System). The shared task attracted 80 registered teams from 12 countries. During the evaluation phase, 30 unique teams submitted entries, with 21 teams officially ranked in Track 1 and 13 in Track 2 following validation filtering, and 20 teams submitting system-description papers. Participating teams employed diverse methodologies, including fine-tuned pretrained language models, prompt-based and retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs), fine-tuned LLMs, and hybrid cascades. Top systems achieved impressive $F_avg2$ scores of 0.8994 on Track1 and 0.9400 on Track2, substantially outperforming the strongest baselines (0.7366 and 0.7475, respectively), where $F_avg2$ denotes the macro-averaged F1 score over the Favor and Against classes. Counterintuitively, performance on the unseen targets was higher than on the related target, a disparity could be driven by extreme target polarization, class imbalance, and dialectal or sarcastic nuance across topics.

title: Razan Alsulieman at StanceEval-2026: Validation Under Target Shift for Arabic Stance Detection
abstract: We describe our systems for both StanceEval- 2026 Arabic stance-detection tracks. Our MARBERT-centered pipeline optimized the primary macro-F1 over AGAINST and FAVOR directly, combining target-aware fine-tuning, probability ensembles, and guarded transfer experiments. We report one official test sub- mission per track. The Track 1 target-routed MARBERT system scored 0.8925 on devel- opment and 0.6743 on the official test set. The Track 2 MARBERT/Fanar/Qwen3 system scored 0.8360 on development and 0.8100 on the official test set. The released Track 1 evaluation input contained only Women Driv- ing, absent from its labeled train and develop- ment targets, making the nominal seen-target track an effective target-transfer test for our system. These results show that validation pro- tocols must reflect the intended target-transfer setting; otherwise, same-target development scores can substantially overstate transfer per- formance.

title: Ahmed Younis at ImageEval 2026 Shared Tasks: The Judge Needs a Prior and the Task Needs a Constraint
abstract: Across two ImageEval 2026 tracks, our best results came from analyzing the evaluation machinery rather than from a stronger model, yielding 1st place on hallucination detection (Task 1b, Modern Standard Arabic) and 4th on CRAI-Bench (Task 2). On CRAI-Bench, which asks systems to predict human cultural-accuracy scores for AI-generated images of Qatari scenes, a blind frequency prior that never looks at an image reaches dev Spearman 0.6878, above the organizers' GPT-4-as-judge baseline of 0.625; adding two vision judges, with blend weights tuned against the global ranking metric rather than by scene-level cross-validation, reaches 0.7806 on the blind test. The weighting correction alone is worth +0.0296 test Spearman, because scene-level cross-validation is structurally blind to the within-cell ranking that judges contribute. On Task 1b, reframing ``label three statements true/false'' as ``select the one grounded statement'' makes invalid labelings structurally impossible and reaches 0.964 combined accuracy on the blind test, against an official baseline of 0.508. A matched-model ablation shows most of that headline gap is the underlying judge, but the constraint still adds +0.026 combined accuracy and eliminates the 4.0\% of items that otherwise receive structurally invalid labelings; meanwhile upgrading to a stronger judge is worth nothing measurable and a three-model vote scored lower.

title: ArabicMTDiagnostics at AlexandriaX-2026: Detecting and Classifying Errors in Dialectal Arabic Machine Translation Outputs
abstract: Dialectal Arabic MT error detection asks a sys tem to locate error spans in a machine trans lation and label each with a linguistic error category. It is hard because the dialects lack a standardised orthography and the error cate gories are severely imbalanced. In Subtask 3 of the AlexandriaX 2026 shared task, the in put is an English sentence and its machine translation into one of five Arabic dialects, and the output is character-level error spans with their LQM categories. The central difficulty is collapse onto the majority sociolinguistics class, 58\% of training spans, leaving rare cat egories undetected. To address this, we fine tune NileChat-3B-Base with QLoRA on a sin gle 8 GB consumer GPU, casting the task as schema-prompted JSON generation and com bining character-position annotations that let the model copy offsets rather than count them, a category guide with one worked example per error type, and self-consistency decoding merging five samples by character-level union voting. Our system scores 0.3484 Overall on the official test set. We report two negative results: early stopping on validation loss de grades performance, since rare categories are acquired only in later epochs, and fine-tuning on the skewed distribution lowers macro-F1 be low the un-fine-tuned baseline until the cate gory guide is added

title: MostafaElAraby at Arabic Segmentationtitle Shared Task 2026: Combining Lexical and Punctuation Evidence across Aligned Text View
abstract: Arabic sentence segmentation without punctuation or paragraph breaks requires predicting boundaries from context. The AraSeg Open Track supplies a parallel punctuated view, but its marks do not consistently indicate sentence endings. We train two CAMeLBERT-MSA ensembles, one for the target No-Punctuation No-Paragraph view and one for the auxiliary No-Paragraph view. A discrete rule combines their boundary decisions with punctuation classes projected onto the target words. Model fitting and selection use only the 174-document official training split: five-fold cross-validation selects the training duration, and out-of-fold predictions calibrate the decoders and fusion rule. Development is reserved for evaluation, and the public test is unused. The system achieves 84.61 document-macro F1 on development and 84.88 on the official blind test, with blind precision of 81.87 and recall of 89.50. It predicts too many boundaries in 80.6\% of development documents, although some of its lowest scores result from missed boundaries.

title: Qahera at IslamicEval 2026: Corpus-Grounded Retrieval and Iterative Harness Search with a 4B-Parameter LLM for Islamic Citation Verification
abstract: We describe the Qahera system for the four IslamicEval 2026 subtasks: (1) detecting Qur'an/Hadith citation spans in LLM-generated Islamic answers, (2) judging citation authenticity, (3) correcting inauthentic citations against reference corpora, and (4) judging whether an authentic citation answers the question asked. Under a 13B-parameter open-model constraint, running entirely on free Kaggle GPUs, we combine a lightweight token-classification model with character-level auxiliary features (Sub-task 1), corpus-grounded fuzzy retrieval (Sub-tasks 2--3), and a 4B-parameter instruction-tuned LLM (Gemma-3-4B) used only where retrieval alone cannot discriminate (Subtasks 3--4). Rather than hand-designing LLM prompts once, we develop them through an iterative propose-evaluate-diagnose search loop that reads full prediction traces after every candidate and hunts for systematic biases before each change. This surfaces small-model failure modes -- a near-universal ``reject'' bias in isolated yes/no verification, and an ``always name something'' bias in numbered-list prompts -- that would otherwise silently cap performance, and shows that validating candidates on small subsets can be actively misleading. Our final system reaches 0.9716 F1 (Subtask 1), 0.906 accuracy (Subtask 2), 0.773 accuracy (Subtask 3), and 0.673 macro-F1 (Subtask 4) on the official test sets.

title: Taqwatech at IslamicEval 2026: Contextual Span Detection and Corpus-Grounded Verification of Islamic Citations
abstract: Reliable use of large language models in religious settings requires more than fluent text, since a generated answer may misquote Qur'anic verses or Hadiths, assign them to the wrong source, or provide an inaccurate narrator chain. This paper presents the Taqwatech systems for Subtasks~1 and~2 of IslamicEval 2026. For Subtask~1, we fine-tune CAMeLBERT-Mix as a BIO sequence-labeling model to detect Ayah, Hadith matn, isnad, and claimed-source spans. The predicted token labels are then converted into the character offsets required by the task. For Subtask~2, we develop a corpus-grounded verification system that combines Arabic normalization, lexical retrieval, character-level TF--IDF, Qur'anic verse matching, source validation, and narrator matching. On the official test set, our systems achieved a character-level macro-F1 score of 0.9683 for Subtask~1 and a macro accuracy of 0.9050 for Subtask~2. The results show strong performance in span detection and Qur'anic citation verification, while isnad verification remains the main area for improvement.

title: AyahVerse at HalluScoring-2026: Category-Aware Arabic Hallucination Detection with Multi-Layer Representations
abstract: We present our submission to HalluScoring 2026, an ArabicNLP shared task on hallucination detection and answer recovery in Arabic LLM outputs. For Track 1, our submitted baseline fine-tunes CAMeLBERT for binary hallucination detection, achieving 0.921 and 0.763 AUC-ROC on the development and test sets of Task 1.1, and 0.749 and 0.729 on Task 1.2, respectively. We further conduct post-submission ablations with intermediate-layer supervision and category embeddings to study their effect on generalization. The combined model achieves 0.929 AUC-ROC on Task 1.1 and 0.777 on Task 1.2 development sets. For Track 2, we separate hallucination detection from answer selection, using CAMeLBERT for detection and a decoder-based, QLoRA-tuned AceGPT-v2-8B-Chat for option selection. The system achieves combined scores of 0.784 on Task 2.1 and 0.829 on Task 2.2 on the validation sets, improving substantially over the corresponding zero-shot baselines.

title: ANLP\_UniSo at KnowledgeGraphEval 2026: Domain-Adaptive Nested Named Entity Recognition for Arabic via GlobalPointer Ensembling
abstract: The ANLP\_UniSo team submitted a system to Subtask 1 (Named Entity Recognition) of KnowledgeGraphEval 2026, which focuses on nested NER in Arabic and evaluates crossdomain and cross-dialect generalization from the Wojood corpus to the multi-domain Konooz benchmark. The system is a combination of an Efficient GlobalPointer decoder with rotary position embeddings and a MARBERT backbone. To reduce the domain gap, first domainadaptive pretraining (DAPT) is performed on unlabeled Konooz text, and then a pseudolabeling self-training stage is applied. A second model based on AraBERT is trained and combined to the other model using a stacking ensemble to improve prediction diversity. As for the Wojood test set, the best ensemble achieves a micro F1 of 0.9288, increasing to 0.9292 when entity-type-specific decision thresholds are used, compared with 0.9211 for the single MARBERT model. On the official blind Konooz test set, however, the submitted system obtains a micro F1 of 0.7106 (macro F1 = 0.6101, weighted F1 = 0.7013, P = 0.8143, R = 0.6304, accuracy = 0.9948). The lower recall suggests that the decoding threshold chosen based on the Wojood validation data was too strict for the domain-shifted Konooz data. the system study the difference and propose a threshold-recalibration strategy to improve the performance under the target-domain distribution.

title: TTLab at Daleel 2026: STAR-Ar, Sequence Tagging for Argument Recognition in Arabic
abstract: Argument Mining (AM) is a critical NLP task that remains significantly under-resourced in Arabic. This paper presents STAR-Ar, a BERT-BiLSTM-CRF architecture for argument discourse detection and classification, as our system for Daleel 2026, the inaugural Arabic argument mining shared task. The task requires the identification and classification of argumentative discourse units (ADUs) in debate and editorial texts. We jointly model these two objectives as a token-level sequence labeling task using a BERT-BiLSTM-CRF architecture that combines contextual transformer embeddings with structural transition constraints to support accurate span detection. STAR-Ar achieves an F1-score of 72.69 on validation and 73.7 on test data. Our domain-specific analysis shows that models trained exclusively on editorials underperform those trained on debates, a disparity we primarily attribute to the smaller size of the editorial dataset.

title: Durham-Jazan at Daleel 2026: Domain-Routed Ensembles, LLM Augmentation, and the Limits of Decision-Rule Tuning for Arabic Argument Mining
abstract: We describe the Durham-Jazan submissions to the Daleel 2026 shared task on Arabic argumentative discourse mining, which comprises multi-label paragraph classification (Task 1) and argumentative span detection (Task 2), each with a Closed and an Open track. Our Task 2 Closed system routes the Modern Standard Arabic editorials to CAMeLBERT and the noisier debate transcripts to MARBERTv2. The Open system blends the two families at character level and adds synthetic training data from a large language model for rare-class generalisation, generated by a segment-concatenation recipe that makes span offsets exact by construction. The Task 1 systems add back-translation, targeted augmentation of the rare classes, and a QLoRA-tuned Qwen3-32B for the editorials. Everything else trains on one 16 GB consumer GPU. Our official test scores are 0.729 and 0.736 overlap-F1 on Task 2 and 0.657 and 0.669 macro-F1 on Task 1 (Closed and Open). We placed first of two on Task 1 Open, first of one on Task 2 Open, fifth of ten on Task 1 Closed, and sixth of eight on Task 2 Closed. Our central finding concerns our own systems on this data. Recalibrating per-class thresholds on validation outputs overfits them. Under a controlled protocol the held-out effect is negative at every tuning-set size we tested, while the apparent in-sample gain shrinks as the tuning set grows. An audit of eighteen interventions from our campaign is consistent with this, though observational. A size-matched study links the editorial deficit that every team showed to the genre composition of the training data. We release our code and synthetic data.

title: BURHAN at Daleel Shared Task Subtask-1: A Multi-Label Transformer Pipeline for Arabic Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification
abstract: This paper presents our system for Task 1 of the Daleel 2026 shared task, which assigns multiple discourse-function labels to Arabic paragraphs from editorials and debate transcripts. We fine-tune a monolingual Arabic encoder (MARBERTv2) with a label-weighted focal loss, multilabel-stratified k-fold crossvalidation, out-of-fold per-label threshold calibration, k-fold ensembling, and a genreconditioning prefix, in a two-stage protocol that first trains on the training split alone and then retrains on training+development. Internal cross-validation macro-F1 rises from 0.667 to 0.680 across the two stages. On the official test set, the system attains micro-F1 = 0.766 and macroF1 = 0.560, with markedly stronger micro-F1 on debate paragraphs (0.825) than editorials (0.633), and a smaller but consistent macro-F1 gap (0.554 vs. 0.456). Assumption is classified most reliably (F1 = 0.88--0.94) and Common Ground least reliably (F1 \leq 0.12), mirroring the low inter-annotator agreement reported for the same category in the source English scheme. We find a \sim0.12 gap between internal cross-validation and official test macro-F1, concentrated in low-support, genre-sensitive categories. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/EidAhmed1/daleel2026_task1_project.

title: Solodiscourse at Daleel 2026: Lexically-Augmented Focal-Loss Ensembling for Arabic Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification
abstract: We describe our submission to Task 1 (Argumentative Discourse Unit Classification) of the Daleel 2026 shared task on Arabic argument mining, in the closed track. Given a paragraph from an Arabic editorial or debate transcript, the task is to predict the multi-label set of argumentative functions it contains, drawn from six classes: common ground, assumption, testimony, statistics, anecdote, and other. Our system fine-tunes a pretrained Arabic encoder, comparing AraBERT, MARBERT, and CAMeLBERT-mix, augmented with a small side-channel of hand-crafted lexical features motivated directly by the task's class definitions (e.g., reporting verbs for testimony, digit/percentage patterns for statistics), trained with a class-balanced focal loss and combined into a 5-fold cross-validation ensemble; CAMeLBERT-mix was selected as the final encoder for all submitted configurations. In the dev phase, our Both-domain configuration achieved an overall macro-F1 of 0.5600 (editorial 0.4350, debate 0.4900). On the official test-phase Codabench leaderboard, our Both-domain configuration achieved an overall macro-F1 of 0.5265 (editorial 0.3838, debate 0.4943), ranking 10th; our Editorial-only configuration reached an overall macro-F1 of 0.4544 (editorial 0.3249, debate 0.4509). We report two findings grounded in these results: overall (pooled) macro-F1 consistently exceeds the macro-F1 computed on either genre subset alone, and our editorial-only model unexpectedly scores higher macro-F1 on the out-of-domain debate subset than on its own in-domain editorial subset. We discuss both as likely artifacts of per-class support sparsity at the smaller genre-subset scale rather than genuine cross-domain superiority, though we did not conduct a formal ablation study or systematic error analysis to confirm this, which we flag as the primary limitation of this report. Our code is available at https://github.com/turab-usmani/daleel-task1-closedtrack.

title: Northwestern at DialectSentEval 2026: A Comparative Study of MARBERTv2 and AraBERT for Arabic Dialect Sentiment Analysis
abstract: This paper describes our submission to Subtask 1 of DialectSentEval 2026, which focuses on three class sentiment classification for Arabic dialectal text. The task aims to classify sentences written in five Arabic dialects into positive, negative, or neutral sentiment categories. We investigate the effectiveness of transformer-based Arabic language models through a series of controlled experiments. Specifically, we compare MARBERTv2 and AraBERT while maintaining identical pre processing, training, and evaluation settings to ensure a fair comparison. In addition, we examine whether explicitly providing dialect information as part of the input improves classification performance.\par Experimental results on an internal validation split show that MARBERTv2 consistently outperforms AraBERT on this task. Furthermore, removing the explicit dialect tag from the input slightly improves performance, suggesting that MARBERTv2 can effectively capture dialect-specific linguistic patterns directly from the sentence. Our best configuration, which uses MARBERTv2 with sentence-only input, achieves a Macro F1-score of 0.9394 and an accuracy of 94.24\%. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of dialect-aware pre-trained language models for Arabic sentiment analysis and establish a strong baseline for the official shared task evaluation.

title: PTUK-NLP at the DialectSentEval 2026 Shared Task: MARBERT-Based Sentiment Classification, Missing-Dialect Effects, and Error Analysis
abstract: We present our system for Subtask~1 (three-class sentiment classification) of the DialectSentEval 2026 shared task, which evaluates five Arabic dialects using the Multi-Dialect-Sent (MDS-3) hotel-review corpus. Our approach fine-tunes MARBERT with a stratified train/validation split and class-weighted cross-entropy loss. On the official test set, our system achieves an F1 score of 0.8175 and an accuracy of 0.8419, ranking 3rd on the official leaderboard. We identify a substantial dialect mismatch in the dataset: the training set contains no Lebanese reviews, while approximately 20\% of the test set is Lebanese. Adding additional Lebanese reviews from OCLAR partially reduces this gap, but does not eliminate it. The error analysis also shows that misclassifications are concentrated in the neutral class and in reviews that express mixed feelings, often with high confidence. These findings highlight the challenges of cross-dialect sentiment classification under unseen-dialect conditions.

title: NAMAA Community at DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 1: Dialect-Aware Arabic Sentiment Classification with Pretrained Transformer Models
abstract: Arabic dialect sentiment analysis is challenging because regional varieties show considerable lexical, morphological, syntactical, and orthographic variation. This paper presents a transformer-based system developed for DialectSentEval 2026 Subtask 1, a three-class sentiment classification task covering Moroccan, Egyptian, Jordanian, and Saudi Arabic. The system independently fine-tunes three pretrained Arabic language models: AraBERTv2, MARBERTv2, and CAMeLBERT, using a common training protocol. The implementation uses an 80/20 stratified train-validation split, a maximum sequence length of 128, a batch size of 16, a learning rate of $2 \times 10^-5$, and focal loss with $\gamma=2$=2. Model selection was conducted based on validation macro F1. Using the published labeled test set, MARBERTv2 achieves the strongest independent result with 94.07\% macro F1, followed by CAMeLBERT at 81.96\% and AraBERTv2 at 79.77\%. The results demonstrate the importance of Arabic pretraining and dialect-oriented representations and establish MARBERTv2 as the strongest standalone backbone in the current system.

title: Lahja at DialectSentEval Shared Task Subtask-1: Seed-Ensembled MARBERT for Multi-Dialect Arabic Sentiment Analysis with Zero-Shot Lebanese Transfer
abstract: Arabic sentiment analysis must cope with dialects that differ in vocabulary, morphology and spelling. Subtask 1 of the DialectSentEval 2026 shared task poses this problem directly: systems label hotel review sentences from five Arabic dialects as positive, negative or neutral, and one dialect (Lebanese) appears only in the test set. In this paper, we describe the Lahja submission. Since the training corpus is small (1,731 sentences) and consists of parallel translations, we treat unreliable measurement (i.e. leaky validation splits and single training runs) rather than model capacity as the main risk. We fine-tune MARBERTv2 under three random seeds, average their softmax outputs, and validate on a split grouped by review identifier so that all dialect versions of a review stay on the same side. The ensemble reached 0.790 macro-F1 on the official test set, ranking 10th of 12 teams, and lost only about two points from validation to test despite the unseen dialect. Our ablations show that the variation between seeds (about 1.5 points) exceeds the effect of orthographic normalisation or class weighting, and that the normalised ensemble, although best on validation, generalised worst on test. We therefore recommend grouped validation and seed-spread reporting as standard practice for small-data shared tasks.

title: ALEXIS at DialectSentEval Subtask 1 Adversarial Training and Iterative Self-Training for Zero-Shot Dialect Sentiment Analysis
abstract: Dialect sentiment analysis asks for the polarity of a sentence written in a regional Arabic variety rather than Modern Standard Arabic. We present a system for Subtask 1 of DialectSentEval built on two observations about the data. First, the task is one of zero-shot transfer rather than classification: the test set introduces Lebanese, a dialect with no labeled training data and the highest out-of-vocabulary rate in the task (52.0\% of word types, against 19.5--41.0\% for the seen dialects). Second, $k$-fold cross-validation cannot see this, since it measures generalization to unseen sentences and never to an unseen dialect. We therefore validate with a leave-one-dialect-out diagnostic and score every component on the official leaderboard. Three dialectally diverse encoders (MARBERTv2, CAMeLBERT-DA, AraBERTv2) are trained with Fast Gradient Method adversarial training, then refined by confidence-filtered self-training on the unlabeled test set and character-level noise augmentation. Adversarial training contributes $+0.040$ Macro F1 over a gold-only ensemble, self-training a further $+0.027$, and per-class pseudo-label filtering $+0.018$. The final system reaches 0.8667 Macro F1, ranking 1st of 12 submissions, 4.6 points above the runner-up.

title: AISA-ArabicFC: The First Shared Task on Arabic Function Calling for Agentic AI Systems
abstract: Function calling connects language models to external tools, but Arabic structured tool use remains insufficiently evaluated. We present , a shared task at ArabicNLP~2026 built around $12,220$ Arabic requests spanning five dialect groups and eight service domains. Each request has four candidate schemas drawn from a registry of 27 tools, including seven tools that never occur as gold calls; 223 requests require abstention. Systems decide whether to call, select a function, and extract its arguments. Two ranked tracks evaluate core calling and reasoning-trace compliance, with a third diagnostic examining dialect robustness. Twenty-two teams submitted to the blind phase, and 21 produced valid predictions on $1,125$ test requests. We analyze 73 submissions and 13 system descriptions. A LoRA-adapted 4B model ranks first on both competition tracks, with scores of 0.9279 and 0.9400, while argument exact match peaks at 0.8816. However, a deterministic rule combining candidate order and released metadata matches the best observed function-name accuracy of 0.9973, limiting what this metric establishes about language understanding. Exact argument extraction provides most of the competitive separation. Maghrebi has the lowest score for every system, although its small test subset and differences in example composition limit interpretation. We provide public task data, a baseline checkpoint, the scorer, and final rankings, and document evaluation shortcuts and remaining reproducibility limitations.[https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuwaiqAcademy/AISA-ArabicFC-Shared-Task]

title: QMUL\_AK at AISA-ArabicFC: Schema-Constrained Function Calling with ALLaM
abstract: We describe the QMUL\_AK submission to AISA-ArabicFC 2026. The system adapts the Arabic-English ALLaM-7B-Instruct model to function calling with low-rank adaptation (LoRA). It combines an Arabic schema-aware prompt, dialect and no-call resampling, a token-weighted training objective, and deterministic validation of generated calls against the candidate tool schema. The same output supports Track A function calling and Track B reasoning-augmented calling. Training uses only the official task data. On the development set, the system achieves 0.9982 function accuracy and 0.8920 argument exact match, corresponding to overall A and B scores of 0.9345 and 0.9454. On the blind test set, the system reaches overall A and B scores of 0.9253 and 0.9380, ranking 3rd on both submission tracks and 1st of 21 teams on the Track C dialect-robustness diagnostic with a macro-averaged score of 0.9075 and the smallest dialect gap in the shared task (0.077). The results show that function selection is nearly saturated, while argument extraction remains the main source of error.

title: Bridging Digital Tools for Linguistic Documentation and Revitalization
abstract: Digital tools serving language revitalization tend to fall into two categories: 1) linguist-oriented documentation tools that prioritize annotation, morphological analysis, and archival preservation, and 2) community-facing applications that emphasize accessibility and language learning. Few systems integrate the former with the latter, and practical barriers --- including the cost of computational expertise, single-user workflows, and limited data governance --- further constrain their utility. These disconnects incur additional development and communication costs for revitalization teams consisting of linguists and community members. We introduce ``langlit'', a collaborative web-based platform that attempts to tailor documentation workflows for the language revitalization context within a single system. The platform integrates a finite-state morphological analyzer with a three-tier human-in-the-loop annotation workflow, searchable corpus interfaces with multiple query modalities, interactive word construction guided by the morphological grammar, corpus-linked hypothesis tracking with provenance, and a grammar-derived editable dictionary. All components share a single underlying FST grammar, and the system supports configurable access controls, collaborative editing, and optional LLM integration with transparent data handling. Designed for redeployment across languages through a modular architecture, ``langlit'' is published as an open-source repository on GitHub. We situate our system within the existing landscape of revitalization tools through a comparative analysis and discuss how integrated, community-informed design can better serve the specific goals of language revitalization.

title: The Power of Simplicity: N-Grams and Transformers in Nahuatl Language Identification
abstract: In the context of real-world language technology applications, the language or variety in which a given text is written is often unknown or uncertain. Yet, this information is crucial in order to adequately select and apply appropriate models or resources. Language identification (LID), or the process of determining the language or variety of a text sample, is thus often an important fundamental task in natural language processing. LID can be particularly challenging when: (1) there are not many labeled texts for training; and (2) similar or related languages are involved, since these may share a number of surface-level features. In this paper, we present an LID system for Nahuatl, a group of closely-related language varieties spoken in Mexico and Central America. Nahuatl LID involves both of the aforementioned challenges: Nahuatl varieties can be quite similar, sharing morphemes and even many lexical items, and there is a relative paucity of representative, variant-labeled Nahuatl text. We describe LID experiments for a total of 11 Nahuatl varieties, achieving generally good results (90.59\% \pm0.09\% in 5-fold cross-validation experiments). Many of the outstanding errors are the result of confusion between three highly similar Huasteca variants.

title: Thinking in Pictures: A Diagnostic Study of Visual vs. Textual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has become a standard technique for eliciting complex reasoning in large language models, and recent work has extended it to vision-language models (VLMs). However, virtually all multimodal CoT methods generate intermediate reasoning steps in natural language, even for inherently visual problems such as spatial reasoning, geometric manipulation, and object tracking. We ask a fundamental question: when should a VLM reason in words, and when should it reason in pictures? We present VisCoT-Diag, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,200 instances across five visual reasoning categories, and compare four CoT paradigms across four VLMs. Our results reveal a striking modality gap: textual CoT degrades performance by up to 17.5\% on spatial transformation and 13.2\% on multi-object tracking, while visual CoT yields gains of up to 23.1\%. We identify three failure modes (spatial state collapse, transformation hallucination, tracking loss) and show that adaptive modality routing achieves 73.1\% accuracy versus 68.9\% for V-CoT-everywhere. We recommend practitioners use visual CoT for spatial tasks and textual CoT for compositional counting.

title: Look Where You're Told: Instruction-Consistent Attention for GUI Grounding
abstract: Visual grounding in graphical user interface (GUI) requires accurate localization of UI elements from natural language instructions. Conventional coordinate generation approaches face inherent limitations, including sensitivity to resolution variations and lack of interpretability. Recently, coordinate-free attention-based methods have emerged as a promising alternative, but these methods supervise attention using only spatial location signals from ground-truth bounding boxes, without ensuring that the learned attention distributions reflect genuine semantic correspondence between the instruction and the attended visual regions. We propose Attention Cycle-Consistency (ACC), a self-supervised regularization framework that enforces bidirectional alignment between visual attention and instruction semantics. ACC introduces two complementary constraints: semantic consistency, which ensures attended visual regions contain sufficient information to reconstruct the original instruction, and spatial consistency, which requires attention distributions to remain invariant when cycled through instruction reconstruction. We further incorporate entropy regularization to encourage spatially concentrated attention. ACC is applicable as a lightweight, model-agnostic regularizer for attention-based coordinate-free grounding methods, adding zero computational overhead at inference as all auxiliary components are discarded after training.

title: VLCE: A Knowledge-Enhanced Framework for Image Description in Disaster Assessment
abstract: General-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) such as LLaVA and QwenVL produce descriptions of disaster imagery that lack domain-specific vocabulary and actionable detail. We propose the Vision-Language Caption Enhancer (), a framework that integrates external semantic knowledge from ConceptNet and WordNet into the caption generation process for post-disaster satellite and UAV imagery. operates in two stages: first, a baseline VLM generates an initial caption conditioned on YOLOv8 object detections; second, a knowledge-enriched sequential model, a CNN-LSTM or a hierarchical cross-modal Transformer, refines the caption using a vocabulary augmented with 1,566 domain-relevant terms extracted from knowledge graphs. We evaluate on two disaster benchmarks: xBD (satellite, 6,369 images, 3 damage classes) and RescueNet (UAV, 4,494 images, 12 damage classes), using CLIPScore for semantic alignment and InfoMetIC for informativeness. On RescueNet with the Transformer decoder, with knowledge graph enrichment produces captions preferred over QwenVL baselines in 95.33\% of image pairs on InfoMetIC and 73.64\% on CLIPScore. Qualitative analysis shows that without knowledge graph integration, generated captions exhibit hallucinations, word repetition, and semantic incoherence, whereas knowledge-enriched captions maintain factual consistency and domain-appropriate vocabulary. intended as a continuous, extensible monitor of differential framing under changing real-world inputs.

title: FADE: Probing the Limits of VLMs on fine-grained OCR
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved remarkable success in semantic visual reasoning, yet their capacity for fine-grained, low-level perception remains critically under-evaluated. This perceptual fragility limits their reliability in noisy, real-world environments where visual signals are degraded. Furthermore, existing benchmarks often entangle visual perception with language priors, masking these underlying deficits. To address this, we introduce the FAint numeric Detection Evaluation (FADE) dataset, a novel evaluation suite designed to probe the limits of zero-shot Optical Character Recognition (OCR) in frontier MLLMs. By embedding synthetic, strictly numerical sequences over cluttered natural backgrounds at varying levels of transparency ($\alpha$), FADE explicitly disentangles pure visual perception from semantic predictability. We evaluate state-of-the-art models including Gemini 3.0, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, and Gemma 3 against a specialized UNet segmentation baseline. Our results reveal a striking limitation in frontier architectures: while they achieve near-perfect transcription at high visibility, their performance collapses under high transparency. Conversely, the UNet pipeline maintains robust spatial grounding, significantly outperforming generalist models at the lowest visibility thresholds. FADE provides a reproducible dataset to expose and diagnose the perceptual breakage points of modern multimodal systems.

title: Systematic Performance Degradation in Indic Vision-Language Models: Evidence from Hindi and Telugu
abstract: With 1.5 billion people speaking over 120 major languages, India exemplifies the challenges of multilingual AI evaluation. Current multilingual VLM benchmarks suffer from unverified auto-translations, narrow task coverage, small sample sizes, and lack of culturally grounded content. We present HinTel-AlignBench, a comprehensive evaluation framework and benchmark for Hindi and Telugu vision-language models with English-aligned samples. Our framework combines semi-automated translation with human verification to generate 4k QA pairs per language across five domains: adapted English datasets (VQAv2, RealWorldQA, CLEVR-Math) and native Indic sets (JEE for STEM, VAANI for cultural grounding). Evaluation of state-of-the-art open and closed-source VLMs reveals consistent performance regression from English to Indic languages, with average drops of 8.3 points for Hindi and 5.5 points for Telugu across four of five tasks. We identify key failure modes and establish reproducible baselines for multilingual multimodal evaluation.

title: Epistemic Twins: Enabling a Symbolic Science of Language Model Knowledge
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are impactful yet opaque artifacts. Subsymbolic by design, they are defined by billions of numeric weights that interact in a largely inscrutable manner. Current analysis paradigms are either black-box benchmarks that test model performance on pre-defined tasks, or mechanistic interpretability approaches that trace back outputs to specific weights. Both analysis methods are limited by the experimenter's hypothesis space - one must know what to look for to find it. In this article, we argue for a third, radically different analysis paradigm: Epistemic Twins. We propose constructing large-scale symbolic approximations of LLMs in human-readable formats. This enables the comprehensive inspection of factual knowledge (or beliefs) inherent in the model without predefining hypotheses, facilitating large-scale auditing towards better understanding and explainability.

title: Edge Knowledge Bases for Sustainable and Explainable AI
abstract: We propose a vision of EdgeKBs(Edge Knowledge Bases) integrating KBs into Edge AI systems. EdgeKBs can infuse commonsense and domain knowledge within Edge devices to guide them while learning from training data. By doing so, we not only bring explainability and performance benefits of KBs to the Edge, but also enable more efficient, sustainable Edge AI systems. We envisage three approaches to develop EdgeKBs: Slicing Dicing; Tailoring to Fit; and Dynamic EdgeKBs. These EdgeKBs will bring Knowledge-Guided Machine Learning (KGML) to the Edge to support next-generation applications, e.g., Physical AI, cobots, and local natural language interfaces.

title: Can We Do Interpretable NLI with Graphs Based on Atomic Propositions?
abstract: While Large Language Model (LLM)-based Natural Language Inference (NLI) systems achieve high accuracy, their decision-making processes lack auditable structures. This paper explores whether NLI can be performed using only interpretable, graph-based representations of evidence. We introduce a fully graph-based pipeline where the classifier never directly processes the input text. Instead, sentences are decomposed into atomic propositions, converted into $ConceptNet$ triples via constrained decoding, and represented as three graphs per pair: premise, hypothesis, and a retrieved $ConceptNet$ subgraph. These graphs are then fed into a fine-tuned 0.8-billion-parameter language model. On the SNLI dataset, our pipeline achieves 89.7\% accuracy, just 1.9 points below an identically trained text-based model. On ANLI, it matches the published performance of $RoBERTa-large$ on rounds R2 and R3 (48.0\% vs.$\ 48.9\%$ and 44.9\% vs.$\ 44.4\%$) but trails by 16 points on R1, resulting in an overall gap of 9 to 14 points compared to its text counterpart. We term this gap the $price of interpretability$ and demonstrate that it stems from representational limitations rather than data constraints. Ablation studies further reveal that graphs and text are complementary: combining both modalities achieves 92.1\% accuracy on SNLI.

title: Schema-Guided Extraction of Interaction Knowledge Bases from Narrative Text: A Folktale Case Study
abstract: We present MAGIC, a six-dimensional framework for extracting structured knowledge bases of hero and magic entity interactions from narrative texts of folktales and fairytales: each interaction between a story's protagonist and a magical helper, villain, or object is decomposed along trigger modality, actor profile and agency balance, interaction mechanics, outcome valence, narrative function, and narrative position. We build an LLM-based extraction pipeline and apply it to a corpus of 1306 folktales collected from around the world, then show the schema supports rich structural analysis: unsupervised clustering over the extracted features recovers five recurring, readily nameable interaction archetypes -- invoked and unsolicited helpers, a morally tested gatekeeper, a hero-controlled magic object, and an adversarial obstacle -- that are stable across the three full-corpus extraction models (0.95 mean cluster-centroid similarity) and cut across both tale type and regional tradition rather than reproducing existing typological catalogues. We further characterize the schema's reliability under LLM extraction (inter-model, not against a human gold standard): parse success and schema-conformance rates, a decomposition of extraction drift into field-confusion versus vocabulary-incompleteness failure modes, and cross-model field-level agreement, which varies substantially across the six dimensions and is sensitive to how many tales are compared across models. Despite this field-level variability, the archetype-level structure remains stable, suggesting that knowledge bases built from LLM extraction should be evaluated at the level of the downstream structure they support.

title: Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction with Calibrated Abstention and Numeric Self-Consistency
abstract: Large language models (LMs) store vast factual knowledge, yet turning it into a reliable, set-valued knowledge base, where a subject may have zero, one, or many objects, remains hard. The AKBC 2026 shared task (5th LM-KBC edition) poses this in a strict closed-book setting: an open-weight model of at most 32B parameters, with no retrieval, no external knowledge, and no fine-tuning. We start from the metric and observe that it rewards abstention: since an empty prediction scores a perfect F1 against an empty gold set, predicting nothing everywhere already reaches 0.169 relation-averaged macro-F1, and on the null-heavy relations even beats the official baseline. We therefore treat when to answer as a first-class decision and build a per-relation pipeline that grounds each prompt in the relation's exact scope, decides abstention from the sampled set rather than by instruction, and takes a median over samples for numeric relations. Our Gemma-4-31B system (30.7B, the strongest in-budget model we could access) scores 0.461/0.488 (relation-averaged/micro) on validation from a single sample, beating the official baseline on five of the six relations, while a smaller 4-bit Qwen2.5-14B, even with self-consistency voting, reaches only 0.415: in this comparison a larger single-sample model outscores a smaller voted one. Generation is cached, so decoding reproduces without a GPU. We release all code, prompts, and cached generations: https://github.com/minhaz-42/lm-kbc-2026

title: A Forced Answer Channel for Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction at LM-KBC 2026
abstract: The AKBC 2026 shared task (Kalo et al., 2026) asks a system to complete the object set of a subject and a relation out of a language model's parameters, with no retrieval, no training, and no more than 32B parameters. Our system drives one 29.6B backbone through three stages. Several elicitation channels per relation build a candidate pool, exhaustive one-token Yes/No probes verify whatever part of the answer space can be enumerated, and a per-relation decision layer emits the object set. The backbone writes a reasoning channel before its user-facing answer, so a probe prompt has to append the answer-channel header before its first generated token is a verdict. Forcing that channel also makes auxiliary generations cheap, which is what puts roughly 26k border probes inside the budget. Most decision constants are fitted on validation gold under a rule that displaces an incumbent only on a strict improvement of more than one row, and the fitting procedure itself is cross-validated, which cut one city gain from +0.070 to +0.020 before it was adopted. The system scores 0.6553 official macro-F1 against 0.6415 for a prompting baseline on the same backbone, and the gap is uneven: the machinery is worth +0.1662 on awards and costs 0.0204 on hasCapacity, where plain prompting wins. We also report the ceiling we could not move. Twenty-one method families have been fitted against hasCapacity and none of them beats a mass vote over the pool. Harvesting the model's own reasoning traces raises pool coverage from 0.582 to 0.724 and converts none of it.

title: Coverage Is Not Knowledge: Why Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction Looks Selection Bound
abstract: This paper describes the first place system of the AKBC 2026 shared task on predicting complete knowledge base entries from language models, built on a single 31.3B parameter base model in completion mode with no training and no retrieval. It scores 0.7060 on the official test set; the runner up scores 0.6908, and a composite taking the best per relation score of every other ranked team would reach 0.7011.\par The largest single improvement I found is not an algorithm. Asking the model to recall facts about an entity before committing to an answer, rather than asking for the answer directly, moved hasArea from 0.8100 to 0.8700. Three earlier configurations, across two frames and two aggregation methods, had all returned exactly 0.8100, which I had read as evidence that the answers were absent from the candidate pool. That reading was incorrect.\par The main analytical result is a correction to how this field measures headroom, and it corrects my own earlier conclusion as much as anyone else's. Oracle coverage analyses report that hasCapacity is selection bound: the recitation frame puts an acceptable answer in the pool for 84.5 percent of validation subjects while the aggregator realises 36.1 percent. That inference does not survive a null control. A pool of one hundred guesses spanning one decade contains about twenty one mutually exclusive 5 percent tolerance windows, so it contains something acceptably close to almost any plausible target whether or not the model knows the answer. Permuting gold values across subjects measures that coincidence rate directly: 0.355 for hasCapacity against 0.031 for hasArea. Chance corrected, the findable headroom beyond the rank one answer falls from 0.443 to 0.203. Three instruments that are not functions of vote frequency then agree that the relation is knowledge bound.

title: Knowledge Base Construction from Language Models: Mechanisms and Calibrations for Multi-Object Relational Extraction under Parameter Budgets
abstract: We describe our system for the AKBC Shared Task 2026, which asks participants to build knowledge base entries from open-weight language models under a strict 32B total-parameter budget, closed-book setting, and no fine-tuning. Our system combines three complementary families of techniques: (i)~diversity-based generation, which uses multi-question paraphrase prompting and temperature sampling with self-consistency voting to maximize recall; (ii)~gold-caliber post-processing, a set of generic rules that align model outputs to the gold annotation caliber (e.g., collapsing regional stock exchanges, filtering contested territories, and calibrating capacity estimates by rounding patterns); and (iii)~confidence-based gating, which uses log-probability signals to reject low-confidence answers and to verify candidates through independent knowledge pathways. On the validation set our best single-model configuration (Mistral-24B, 24B parameters) reaches a macro-F1 of 0.6562. We additionally analyze which strategies transfer across base models and which fail, providing a practical recipe for closed-book KB construction within tight parameter budgets.[Code is available at https://github.com/LexieeWei/akbc2026.]

title: Exemplars Primarily Shift Retrieval, Verification Instructions Can Shift Rejection: An Anatomy of Inference-Time Interventions for Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction
abstract: We describe our AKBC 2026 closed-book knowledge base construction system: Gemma-3-27B-pt, raw text completion, 20 candidates per query, and relation-specific aggregation without an arbiter. It uses 27.4B parameters and scores 0.6670 row-averaged Macro F1 on the official test, placing sixth. Experiments distinguish this final pipeline from an earlier Mistral system with an 8B arbiter. Backbone and access format outweighed prompt-level interventions: under matched prompt formats, the pretrained checkpoint exceeds its instruction-tuned sibling by 0.11 on validation. Numeric example configurations primarily shift retrieval; procedural wording with five added JSON examples changes the selected answers by only one row. Verification instructions can shift rejection. A biography-first city prompt format affects both, raising validation F1 from 0.55 to 0.61 at a fixed vote gate. Gating, information outside the model, and seed stability help interpret transfer. These findings have counterexamples; leaderboard comparisons describe development outcomes, not an untouched final evaluation.

title: MuseList: Confidence-Gated Multi-Surface Recall for Closed-Book Knowledge Base Construction
abstract: Knowledge base construction requires complete answer sets, not just one plausible fact. We present MuseList, a closed-book system for the six-relation AKBC Shared Task 2026. A single open-weight 29.8B-parameter Muse Glimmer model generates candidate answers in several formats, such as recipient lists, recipient--year tables, and venue records. All such records are model-generated; the system retrieves no external documents. Relation-specific rules combine these candidates, select numerical answers using token-level confidence signals, and check proposed reciprocal borders with three separately prompted roles. The complete system scores 0.6700 hidden-test macro-F1 and ranks fourth among twelve systems. Its development validation score is 0.69160; this split informed method selection and is not an untouched evaluation. We describe the method and release an archive that reconstructs the scored submission exactly. Fresh-call support is separate and partial: it regenerates later-stage responses, not an end-to-end submission.

title: CoRe: Construct-versus-Recall Routing for Knowledge Base Construction Under a Parameter Budget
abstract: We report a system for the LM-KBC shared task under a strict single-repository parameter budget of 32B, which rules out both model ensembling and scaling to a larger model. Starting from a rationalized chain-of-thought (CoT) pipeline that reached macro-F1 0.522 with Gemma-4-31B-it, we show that swapping to a smaller, differently-trained model (Qwen3.5-27B) under an identical pipeline recovers 24 percentage points of exact-match accuracy on a purely numeric relation (surface area), while costing accuracy on relations requiring broad factual recall. This shows that parametric knowledge coverage, not reasoning capability, is the limiting factor at this model scale. We then present four negative or reversed results (self-consistency sampling on numeric relations, a confabulation-guard prompt, and two cases of non-comparable validation splits) as diagnostic evidence for why scaffolding choices that help one relation type hurt another. We introduce CoRe routing (Construct versus Recall), which assigns each relation to CoT or direct answering according to whether its answer must be constructed or merely recalled. CoRe reaches macro-F1 0.548 on validation and 0.541 on the test split.

title: DataMind at AKBC Shared Task 2026: Relation-Specific Multiple Prompting for Closed-Book Knowledge Base Completion
abstract: We describe a system for the AKBC Shared Task 2026. The task is to predict complete sets of knowledge base objects from parametric memory alone, with no retrieval and no fine-tuning, across six relations and within a 32B parameter budget. Our system combines relation-specific multiple prompting, consistency-based aggregation, and error-driven prompt refinement. For each relation, multiple prompt variants and samples elicit complementary predictions, with cross-prompt agreement reducing wording-specific errors and cross-sample agreement filtering unstable guesses. Aggregation is tailored to each relation, including cluster-median aggregation for numeric values and voting for categorical and set-valued outputs. The system achieves a validation macro-F1 of 0.5577 and a test macro-F1 of 0.5699, compared to organizer baselines of 0.3131 (validation) and 0.2964 (test).

title: Relation-Specific Elicitation of a Base Model under a 32B Closed-Book Budget for LM-KBC 2026
abstract: We describe a system for the LM-KBC 2026 shared task on closed-book knowledge base construction. Given a subject and relation, the system tries to predict all corresponding objects without retrieval or additional training and remains within the 32-billion-parameter limit. The system uses the base model gemma-4-31B with separate prompting and aggregation rules for six relations; few-shot demonstrations and selection thresholds come from the train set and are checked on the validation set. It obtains 0.6975 global F1 on the official validation set, compared with 0.308 for the organiser baseline on validation. The largest per-relation gains over our earlier baseline configuration come from a company-listing prompt with explicit abstention and a log-stratified area prompt, plus a vote-share abstention threshold for empty-heavy relations (like personHasCityOfDeath) that recovers most of the empty-case precision. Across more than 30 prompting, verification, and aggregation configurations, further inference rarely recovers facts that are absent from the generated candidates. These results indicate that relation-specific elicitation improves closed-book extraction, while candidate coverage and selection remain the main limitations. Code, prompts, and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ruggsea/lmkbc2026-submission.

title: Stochastic Constrained Test Assembly for AI-Enabled Assessment Systems
abstract: Test assembly, the process of constructing a complete test form from an item pool subject to blueprint constraints, has traditionally been treated as a static optimization problem. In AI-enabled assessment environments, however, item pools evolve continuously as newly generated items enter with uncertain psychometric parameters, and delivery is on demand. These conditions make test assembly a sequential decision-making problem under uncertainty: which form should be deployed now, given current but incomplete knowledge of item quality, to simultaneously maximize measurement precision, satisfy content-blueprint constraints, maintain pool sustainability, and accelerate calibration of uncertain new items? This paper proposes the Stochastic Constrained Hybrid (SCH) framework as a principled answer to this question. SCH recasts form-level assembly as a multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem with Fisher information as the reward, extending recent item-level approaches in computerized adaptive testing (CAT) to the form-level setting. A simulation study comparing six test assembly methods is also presented. The main contribution of this paper is a framework for incorporating items with uncertain parameters into the automatic test assembly process for linear test forms.

title: How Much Does Hyperparameter Tuning Actually Help? An Efficiency Survey for Fine-Tuning Transformers to Score Mathematics-Explanation Items
abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models for constructed-response items often begins with a hyperparameter grid search using k-fold cross-validation. We study how much that search actually helps by fine-tuning two encoders---MathBERT, a smaller math-focused model, and DeBERTa-v3-large, a larger general-purpose model---to score 18 math-explanation items from a state-wide assessment. Crossing learning rate, weight decay, and label smoothing over two epochs and five folds (1,800 model-fold runs), we compare each model's tuning gain directly against fold-to-fold noise via a gain-to-noise ratio. Gains were small relative to fold noise for both encoders: MathBERT's ratio fell below one (0.90), and DeBERTa's nominally higher ratio (1.42) traced to a handful of divergent fits rather than an informative search landscape. Weight decay and label smoothing were effectively inert, leaving learning rate as the only hyperparameter worth checking---though even for learning rate the best configurations offered small performance gains over a reasonable default. We accordingly recommend a lean workflow that fixes the inert hyperparameters to sensible defaults, runs a narrow learning-rate search extended modestly upward, and increases the epoch budget with early stopping, substantially reducing training compute without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Identifying Communication Profiles from Physician--Patient Conversations Using Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to score clinical communication, but validation is often limited to individual checklist items or total scores. These measures may not capture how communication behaviors occur together within a transcript. We therefore examine communication profiles: recurring combinations of behaviors that characterize different patterns of clinician communication and may support more targeted formative feedback. We analyzed 213 simulated respiratory OSCE transcripts rated on 15 binary Kalamazoo-derived communication items and compared final human ratings with GPT-4o, GPT-o3, and GPT-5.6 Sol. Raw item-level agreement was relatively high overall, but varied substantially across behaviors and was lower for several judgment-intensive items used for profile modeling. Bayesian latent-class analysis identified three stable human-derived profiles. Although the LLM-derived profiles showed broadly similar item-probability patterns, the models frequently assigned individual transcripts to different profiles than the human ratings. These findings show that agreement on individual communication skills does not necessarily translate into agreement on higher-level communication profiles. If LLMs are used to provide profile-based feedback, validation should therefore include profile-level agreement in addition to item-level performance.

title: Validating LLM-Rated Item Features for Explanatory Item Response Models
abstract: Explanatory item response models let test de- velopers anticipate item difficulty from item design, but they depend on subject-matter ex- perts rating every item on every hypothesized feature---a step that is slow, costly, and the practical bottleneck limiting how many items can be modeled. We ask whether large lan- guage models can supply those ratings. Four trained experts and six LLMs independently rated 15 grade-5 mathematics items on six psy- chometric features. We evaluate the LLM rat- ings twice: against the human consensus using quadratic-weighted $\kappa$and mixed-effects mod- els, and against 1,452 student responses by us- ing each source's ratings as the design matrix of a linear logistic test model (LLTM) bench- marked against a Rasch baseline. Claude Opus 4.7 performed best in recovering the item dif- ficulty (r = 0.89), however, the human con- sensus against which agreement is measured performs worst at recovering Rasch difficulty (r = 0.33) compared to the rest of the LLMs. The reason is visible in the expert panel it- self: inter-rater Fleiss' $\kappa$is at or below chance on three of six features, so the consensus is a noisy reference rather than ground truth. We also identify two failure modes (zero-variance and perfect collinearity) that agreement statis- tics cannot detect but make a feature unusable as an LLTM covariate. We argue that agree- ment should be reported alongside criterion- referenced recovery of item parameters, not in place of it.

title: Assessing Small Language Models as Decimal-Arithmetic Tutors: A Measurement Framework
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly proposed for educational use because they promise lower cost, offline deployment, and stronger data privacy. We report an exploratory evaluation of three sub-2B-parameter models on example-based decimal-arithmetic tutoring. Across structured interactions, all three produced fluent, confident output that masked unstable pedagogy and frequent mathematical errors even on elementary decimal addition and place-value tasks. Building on these observations, we describe an emerging interaction-based measurement framework intended to support more defensible readiness decisions about SLMs as math tutors.

title: Beyond the Grid: Auditing Code-Editing Search for Automated Essay Scoring
abstract: Code-editing language-model agents can change training choices beyond the hyper- parameter grids tested in automated essay scoring. Comparing these approaches requires distinguishing gains from a broader search space from evidence of a better search procedure. We compare code-editing agents with grid-restricted search, including random search, in two studies on ASAP-AES with nominally matched 12-hour search budgets. Code-editing produced the configuration with the highest test quadratic-weighted kappa (QWK) point estimate in each primary comparison. However, random search over a grid built afterwards around the Study 2 agent's backbone, input length and head rule recovered most of its gain over BERT. Requiring a minimum validation-score improvement to accept a trial also left the accepted configuration's validation score below the highest recorded valid validation score in every run that accepted a trial under this rule. The primary comparisons use one search run per condition, and some test folds reused essays involved in configuration selection, so these results compare selected configurations without establishing search-procedure superiority. These findings motivate reporting the available search choices and both accepted and best-scoring trials, and evaluating search procedures through repeated runs on data independent of configuration selection.
