title: Private Evaluation Protocol: Contamination-Resistant Black-Box Evaluation via Public-Slice Surrogates
abstract: Existing paradigms for black-box LLM evaluation by independent third parties share a structural weakness: the testing benchmark must reach the model being evaluated, enabling model developers to game future evaluations through logging or retraining. Ideally, rigorous evaluation would grant evaluators direct access to the model so testing can occur without exposing benchmark contents. However, proprietary black-box models cannot be released to external evaluators, creating a fundamental barrier to independent evaluation. To address this gap, we propose the Private Evaluation Protocol (PEP), a surrogate-based framework for independent evaluation of black-box models without sending the private benchmark to the model developer. PEP releases a small public slice of a held-out benchmark, queries the target model only on that slice, and trains a surrogate from the resulting responses, balancing fidelity to the target model against leakage of the private remainder over a tunable revelation budget. Across six benchmarks, composite leakage scores reliably predict behavioral exposure (r=0.788), and fine-tuned surrogates reach 0.85--0.90 agreement on template-heavy datasets while plateauing below 0.73 on reasoning-heavy datasets. The optimal revelation budget is dataset-dependent, and PEP estimates black-box performance with 5.88 percentage-point MAE, showing the feasibility of private surrogate-based evaluation for structured tasks while protecting the privacy of the held-out benchmark.

title: The Same Answer Every Time: Auditing Small Medical LLM Agents
abstract: We investigate how small open-weight language models make decisions in medical tasks and whether their failures also occur in other settings. We evaluated nine models on wearable fatigue and intensive-care tasks, where they chose among six recommendations, including continued monitoring. We then extended testing to a non-medical tool router and subsets of the Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard and JSONSchemaBench. We introduce the Minimum Viable Audit (MVA) to examine which actions models choose, whether their responses contain usable decisions, and whether they copy prompt content. Comparisons across tasks help establish where these behaviors recur. Under the baseline intensive-care prompt, MedGemma chose continued monitoring in all 450 attempts, achieving 33.3\% accuracy. On the router, it used all six tools and answered 144 of 150 requests correctly. Meditron-7B produced unusable responses and copied prompt content across intensive-care monitoring and the non-medical evaluations at both four-bit and eight-bit quantization. MedGemma's results motivate checking the medical instructions. Meditron's recurring failures warrant checking the model configuration and how outputs are generated. Differences between tasks and mismatches between medical prompts and scoring rules limit conclusions about the causes of these failures. We recommend reporting selected actions, invalid and copied responses, and results for each prompt condition alongside accuracy.

title: Multidimensional Consistency Improves Reasoning in Language Models
abstract: While Large language models (LLMs) have proved able to address some complex reasoning tasks, we also know that they are highly sensitive to input variation, which can lead to different solution paths and final answers. Answer consistency across input variations can thus be taken as a sign of stronger confidence. Leveraging this aspect, we introduce a framework where models are systematically pushed to diversify solution paths towards a final answer, thereby testing them for answer consistency across multiple input variations. Focusing on math problems, we induce variations in (i) order of shots in prompt, (ii) problem phrasing, and (iii) languages used. Experiments on a wide range of open-source LLMs of various sizes show that reasoning consistency differs by variation dimension, and that by aggregating consistency across dimensions, our framework enhances mathematical reasoning performance on monolingual datasets GSM8K and MATH500, and the multilingual dataset MGSM. We also discuss the different efficacy of the types of variations induced and how they could be further leveraged in future work.

title: CriticGen: Generation-Aware Evaluation as Actionable Feedback
abstract: Current evaluation methods for large language models are coarse-grained and decoupled from generation, producing generic explanations that fail to provide actionable feedback for model improvement. We propose CriticGen, a fine-grained, generation-aware evaluation framework that turns evaluation into actionable control for answer improvement. CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria, then uses the induced rubric to jointly produce a score, a reason, an executable refinement suggestion, and a refined answer. Experiments show that fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable. CriticGen improves human-rated rubric relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24. On the score-consensus-filtered RefineData test set, the best CriticGen variant reaches 0.9556/0.9560 Pearson/Spearman agreement with the reference scores and improves reason/suggestion F1 to 0.7554/0.7900. Independent validation provides additional support: on 180 human-scored instances, CriticGen-Qwen2.5-7B obtains higher observed score correlations than GPT-5, with 0.8868/0.8969 Pearson/Spearman versus 0.8542/0.8615. Crucially, its feedback translates into substantial answer improvement, raising accuracy from 45.36\% to 91.26\% on 5,000 examples with reliable gold answers, with 47.30\% of answers corrected from Wrong$\rightarrow$Right and only 1.40\% degraded from Right$\rightarrow$Wrong.

title: LLM-Generated Social-Desirability Ratings for Forced-Choice Questionnaire Construction: A Preregistered Downstream Validation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly produce evaluative judgments, but rating-level human--model agreement does not establish whether they can replace human inputs in a downstream task. Using HEXACO personality items as a case study, we conduct a preregistered three-stage validation of whether LLM-generated social-desirability ratings can serve as inputs to forced-choice scale construction, a psychometric task that requires costly human ratings. In Stage I, three LLMs served as raters of item-level social desirability for sentence- and adjective-format items, with human ratings serving as references. In Stage II, human- and LLM-based ratings were entered into the same constrained optimization procedure. In Stage III, 400 participants completed the resulting forms, and latent trait estimates were compared using graded Thurstonian item response theory. LLM ratings showed strong item-level correspondence with human ratings (sentence: $r = 0.942$--0.963; adjective: $r = 0.979$--0.980), but optimized forms showed partial item overlap and sparse exact pair overlap. Despite these design differences, LLM-based forms produced latent trait estimates that closely matched those from human-based forms (mean $r = 0.815$ for sentence items and 0.768 for adjective items). These results support the conditional use of LLM-generated ratings as scalable construction inputs while showing why downstream validation is necessary.

title: Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention for Conversational LLMs
abstract: Large language models often lose track of persistent instructions and relevant information as multi-turn conversations grow. We study this cumulative contextual decay through three related failure modes: attention pollution, dilution, and drift. We propose REA (Role-aware Heuristic Episodic Attention), a context-management framework that assigns different persistence and representation policies to instructions and episodic interactions. Instructional Memory retains identified global constraints in a dedicated prefix. Episodic Memory preserves user inputs and compresses model replies, while heuristic retrieval selects raw text, compressed representations, or omission for each historical turn. On Long-MT-Bench+, REA improves the judge score from 6.32 to 7.36 on a 10-point scale, a 16.5\% relative gain over the Vanilla baseline, and reduces average latency by 2.91\texttimes. Additional evaluations show aggregate gains on three backbones spanning 1.7B--7B parameters and on Chinese and English role-playing tasks. These results support role-aware context management as a practical approach to maintaining conversational continuity and instruction adherence.

title: KoEVD: A Korean Benchmark for Metadata-Conditioned Multi-Stage LLM Safety Evaluation
abstract: Large language model (LLM) safety benchmarks often evaluate input risk, response selection, generation, and tool use separately, making comparisons across tasks difficult. We introduce KoEVD (Korean Ethical Violation Dataset), which links five evaluation and analysis tasks through annotated Korean source utterances: input-risk judgment, candidate-response selection, generation safety, response-strategy analysis, and non-executable mock-tool selection. The tasks share source IDs, with task-specific subsets and candidate sampling where required. Built through an approximately 3.5-year human-governed, AI-assisted process, KoEVD contains 13,552 curated user utterances and 71,395 linked response candidates. Across 12 open-weight and commercial models, observed task profiles differ, and aggregate scores obscure variation across severity, explicitness, utterance type, and topic. In matched generation and mock-tool-selection cases, responses classified as safe coexist with unsafe mock-tool choices; pooled unsafe-call rates are 9.73\% and 9.31\% for the classifier-safe and classifier-unsafe groups, respectively, with framing-specific differences. These diagnostic measurements do not establish real-world safety. KoEVD supports detailed Korean safety analysis through contextual annotations and source-linked comparisons.

title: ConceptWeave: Concept-Driven Prompting through Adaptive Semantic Infilling
abstract: Conventional prompting and prompt-based finetuning offer only weak semantic structure, leaving models to derive task-specific reasoning from limited cues. Existing techniques, such as using demonstrations, chain-of-thought prompting, or retrieval augmentation, can improve performance, but often at the cost of longer, more redundant prompts, higher inference overhead, and reliance on external knowledge sources. We present ConceptWeave, a novel concept-centric prompt-based finetuning approach built on adaptive semantic infilling. Instead of depending on external resources, it extracts concise, task-relevant concepts directly from a small portion of downstream data and organizes them into a dynamically evolving hierarchical memory. During fine-tuning, ConceptWeave identifies informative spans in the input through semantic alignment and augments them with corresponding concept representations, enabling fine-grained, localized conditioning of the model. As training progresses, the concepts are continuously refined and structured into a hierarchy that supports efficient retrieval while preserving semantic richness and scalability. We validate ConceptWeave across a range of NLP tasks, including misinformation detection, question answering, sentiment analysis, and hate speech classification, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines and recent state-of-the-art methods.

title: What Makes User Reactions Useful for Fake News Detection?
abstract: Fake news detection is often treated as a content-centered task, yet social media posts are embedded in user reactions that express skepticism, endorsement, correction, ridicule, and affective responses. This paper asks what makes user reactions useful for fake news detection. We study performance according to different dimensions: text only, emotions in comments, and number of available comments. We study this question across Fakeddit and Weibo20 under both standard and temporal splits (in a temporal split, most recent posts are included in the testing split). Robustness of results is measured across two encoder families (BERT-base, RoBERTa-base) and two English emotion taxonomies (dair-ai/emotion, GoEmotions). Across these configurations, comment-only representations outperform post-only baselines in most evaluation regimes, though this gain depends on dataset, split, and number of available comments. Emotion-fine-tuned comment encoders produce a temporal-shift-specific significant benefit compared to non-temporal splits.\par We compare post-only representations, generic comment representations, emotion-fine-tuned comment representations, and post--reaction fusion models, while varying comment availability, showing that a minimum number of comments is necessary to improve detection of fakes. In addition, we show that fine-tuning comment or reaction-encoders on relevant auxiliary tasks such as emotions has a significant impact on the distribution of embeddings of fake and real posts in their representation space.\par In light of these findings, we believe that user responses---and their emotional structure for example---should be taken into account when detecting fake news or compiling datasets for this purpose.

title: JanusPO: Asymmetric Clip and KL for Entropy-Stable Group Policy Optimization in Tool-Augmented LLM Reasoning
abstract: Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO, DAPO, ARPO) has become the dominant recipe for RL fine-tuning of reasoning LLMs, yet in the resource-constrained regime most practitioners train in (a single GPU, small batches) it consistently suffers from rapid entropy collapse that kills exploration, together with sparse credit assignment in long rollouts, which is most extreme under multi-turn tool use but already present in long single-turn chain-of-thought. We address both failure modes with JANUSPO, a drop-in GRPO modification that introduces asymmetric PPO clipping $\epsilon_+<\epsilon_-$ to tolerate larger downward than upward updates, pairs it with an asymmetric KL schedule $\beta_pos<\beta_neg$ that doubles as a free entropy regulator without any explicit upper bound, and redistributes the terminal reward through a turn-weighted decomposition $w_t(n)$ that generalises naturally from single-turn CoT to multi-turn rollouts. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct / GSM8K, JANUSPO improves from 74.8\% to 84.3$\pm$0.2\% (mean$\pm$std over 2 seeds) across 14 controlled ablations, and the same recipe lifts 7B from 85.3\% to 93.6\% with no hyper-parameter retuning. On multi-turn DeepSearch (103 GAIA + 100 HLE), SFT-warmup-then-JANUSPO is the only RL recipe whose paired comparison against SFT survives best@8 outlier verification, achieving strict dominance on all four reward and F1 columns while a matched-init GRPO baseline's apparent F1 wins collapse to 0\%. Beyond this main result, we document a systematic negative finding: SFT warm-up is a necessary precondition for GRPO-style multi-turn RL on format-unaware base models.

title: Explainable Multimodal Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Dependency-guided Large Language Model
abstract: Multimodal aspect-based sentiment analysis (MABSA) aims to identify aspect-level sentiments by jointly modeling textual and visual information, which is essential for fine-grained opinion understanding in social media. Existing approaches mainly rely on discriminative classification with complex multimodal fusion, yet lacking explicit sentiment explainability. In this paper, we reformulate MABSA as a generative and explainable task, proposing a unified framework that simultaneously predicts aspect-level sentiment and generates natural language explanations. Based on multimodal large language models (MLLMs), our approach employs a prompt-based generative paradigm, jointly producing sentiment and explanation. To further enhance aspect-oriented reasoning capabilities, we propose a dependency-syntax-guided sentiment cue strategy. This strategy prunes and textualizes the aspect-centered dependency syntax tree, guiding the model to distinguish different sentiment aspects and enhancing its explainability. To enable explainability, we use MLLMs to construct new datasets with sentiment explanations to fine-tune. Experiments show that our approach not only achieves consistent gains in sentiment classification accuracy, but also produces faithful, aspect-grounded explanations.

title: All Verdicts are Not Equal: Rethinking LLM Judge Reliability
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge is the standard paradigm for NLP evaluation, yet its systemic reliability remains poorly understood despite being widely treated as a deterministic ground truth. We present a comprehensive reliability audit, stress-testing six frontier models across four benchmarks, five prompt formats, two presentation orders, three sampling temperatures, and ten repetitions per condition. Our empirical analysis reveals severe vulnerabilities: verdicts change across identical replications at temperature zero, position-order swaps flip the majority of verdicts on challenging tasks, and the most deterministic judge achieves perfect consistency by trivially repeating incorrect verdicts, agreeing with ground truth only 51\% of the time. To formalize these multi-faceted failure modes, we introduce the trustworthy verdict rate ($T$), a unified metric capturing the joint probability that an evaluation is reproducible, order-invariant, and accurate. Using $T$ , we derive a theoretical upper bound on accuracy imposed by position bias and show that reliability is item-specific rather than model-level. Finally, we demonstrate that shifting from pairwise win-rate to holistic rubric scoring improves trustworthiness more than any single-format prompting intervention, offering an actionable framework for robust NLP evaluation.

title: Forgetting Only What Matters: Layer-Selective Unlearning toward Robust LLMs
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or otherwise undesirable training content, creating privacy, safety, and regulatory concerns. Machine unlearning offers a practical alternative to full retraining, but many existing methods apply broad or fixed parameter updates that can degrade utility and remain brittle under deployment changes such as post-training quantization, where forgotten knowledge may partially re-emerge.\par We propose Forgetting Only What Matters via Unlearning Layers (FOM-UL), a layer-level unlearning framework that selects transformer layers using a forget-to-retain significance score. This score identifies layers with high influence on the forget set and low sensitivity to the retain set, allowing FOM-UL to concentrate updates where they are most effective while leaving most of the model unchanged. This targeted update strategy improves the forgetting-utility trade-off and provides an empirical path toward quantization-resilient unlearning by reducing the chance that small, diffuse updates are erased by low-bit rounding.\par Across TOFU, KnowUnDo, and MUSE-style evaluations, FOM-UL reduces residual memorization compared with strong GA, NPO, KLD, SURE, ReLearn, and LUNAR-based baselines while preserving retain-set utility close to the vanilla model. Under 8-bit and 4-bit post-training quantization, FOM-UL maintains a favorable forgetting-utility trade-off, combining competitive memorization suppression with stronger retained utility. Overall, FOM-UL provides an efficient unlearning strategy that improves targeted forgetting, utility preservation, and deployment robustness without claiming formal guarantees of erasure.

title: A Pre-Training Analogue of Grokking in Language Models: Tracing Delayed Grammatical Generalization
abstract: Grokking, the phenomenon in which neural networks generalize long after fitting their training data, has been studied in supervised settings on many epochs. LLM pre-training instead involves next-token prediction over an unlabeled corpus, with limited data repetition and no explicit train/validation split. To address this, we propose an exposure-based framework that enables the study of grokking-like dynamics during LLM pre-training. We ground our evaluation in BLiMP minimal pairs, which provide controlled grammatical contrasts. For every BLiMP minimal pair, we identify a critical phrase, the smallest continuous span that captures the grammatical contrast and the phenomenon-relevant context. Examples whose critical phrase appears in the pre-training window are assigned to the proxy-train split; the remaining examples are assigned to the proxy-validation split. Across five grammatical phenomena, we observe delayed generalization. Analyzing pre-training checkpoints before and after generalization shows that grammatical concept vectors become more predictive of grammatical acceptability and occupy a higher-dimensional subspace after generalization. We also find that attention from the critical token to the relevant context token is concentrated in a small number of heads.

title: Reasoning-Based Personalized Generation for Sparse Users
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) personalization holds great promise for tailoring responses by leveraging personal context and history. However, real-world users usually possess sparse interaction histories with limited personal context, such as cold-start users in social platforms and newly registered customers in online E-commerce platforms, compromising the LLM-based personalized generation. To address this challenge, we introduce GraSPer (Graph-based Sparse Personalized Reasoning), a novel framework for enhancing personalized text generation under sparse context. GraSPer first augments user context by predicting items that the user would likely interact with in the future. With reasoning alignment, it then generates texts for these interactions to enrich the augmented context. In the end, it generates personalized outputs conditioned on both the real and synthetic histories, ensuring alignment with user style and preferences. Extensive experiments on three benchmark personalized generation datasets show that GraSPer achieves significant performance gain, substantially improving personalization in sparse user context settings.

title: The bias is in the generator: locating medical chain-of-thought subgroup gaps upstream of the verifier
abstract: Verifier-guided best-of-$N$ decoding has two stages: a generator samples candidate chains of thought, and a verifier selects among them. A subgroup disparity may already be present in the generator's candidates or be amplified during selection. We separate the two stages using adversarial demographic counterfactuals of medical exam questions. On HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, a substantial race accuracy gap is already present in a single sampled response, before verifier selection. Across seven generators, only Gemma-3-27B-it under Skywork-RM shows significant verifier-induced amplification after multiple-testing correction. Even an oracle selector leaves a residual gap on every medical generator analyzed, showing that correct answers are less often available for one subgroup. Counterfactually paired low-rank adaptation (LoRA) of the generator reduces the single-sample gap on two medical models, although on HuatuoGPT-o1-8B the reduction does not persist after self-judge selection. Single-variant controls indicate that the single-sample reduction is not explained by additional training steps alone. A short fairness instruction modestly reduces the single-sample gap, and a direct preference optimization (DPO) variant of the paired training also reduces it and, on HuatuoGPT-o1-8B, keeps race mention near its baseline rate. For the medical generators studied, candidate generation rather than inference-time selection is the primary locus for mitigating this gap.

title: Do Correctness Probes Transfer? A Cross-Family Study of LLM Hidden States
abstract: Linear probes on language-model hidden states can predict output correctness, but it remains unclear whether they capture transferable correctness representations. We study out-of-distribution correctness-probe transfer across seven datasets, four task families, and three open-weight LLMs: Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B, with all findings validated across five random seeds. Within-family transfer is consistently stronger than cross-family transfer (gap 0.075 AUC), with code generation showing the clearest pattern across MBPP-test, MBPP-train, and HumanEval. We further find that probe weight directions are nearly orthogonal across most dataset pairs despite strong predictive transfer, suggesting that probes do not encode a single canonical correctness direction. Comparing probes to logprob confidence baselines, we find probe advantage is concentrated in in-domain and within-family transfer cells. We also identify a layer-selection confound where early-layer shortcuts can appear transferable in-domain but fail cross-source. Overall, correctness probes transfer selectively rather than universally, making them most useful in-domain and within task families.

title: A Systematic Review of Meta-Reasoning for Large Reasoning Models
abstract: In this paper, we survey recent advances in meta-reasoning for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). Although LRMs have made remarkable progress, they face critical limitations including overthinking on simple queries, under-thinking on complex problems, and ineffective exploration lacking strategic direction. We examine how meta-reasoning addresses these challenges by providing the necessary mechanisms to dynamically regulate and optimize the reasoning process, and propose a framework to categorize existing studies into three core components: the monitor which provides self-perception of the reasoning state, the controller which dictates the meta-policy for regulating actions, and the mechanism which executes the algorithmic mapping between them. By systematically reviewing these developments and foundational challenges, we aim to map the current landscape and identify promising directions for creating more adaptive, efficient, and self-regulating reasoning systems.

title: Domain-Agnostic Neural Topic Modeling with Contextual Token-Level Semantic Graph Representation
abstract: PLM-powered neural topic models depend on general-domain pre-training, leading to degraded topic interpretability on specialized corpora. The root cause is geometric: domain-specific terms unseen during pre-training collapse into an indistinguishable region of the embedding space, and neither domain-specific re-training, word-level graph enrichment, nor parameter-efficient fine-tuning can restructure this space without inheriting the capacity ceiling of the underlying encoder. Our key insight is that a learnable graph layer operating on token-level PLM embeddings can acquire corpus-specific semantic structure that the frozen encoder lacks, because token-level graphs preserve document-local context that word-level representations discard and joint optimization with the topic objective reshapes embedding geometry directly from target-domain evidence. We instantiate this insight as DARTopic, a domain-agnostic framework that constructs token-level semantic graphs from frozen PLM embeddings and jointly trains a GNN encoder with variational topic inference. Across three benchmarks spanning general, biomedical, and legal domains, DARTopic consistently outperforms strong baselines in topic coherence and document clustering without any encoder fine-tuning, while demonstrating robustness to PLM choice and favorable runtime efficiency over fine-tuning-based alternatives.

title: Structural vs Cultural Reasoning: Reliability Limits of LLM-as-a-Judge in Multilingual Evaluation
abstract: LLM-as-a-Judge has emerged as a scalable alternative to human evaluation in multilingual cultural reasoning, yet its reliability for culturally grounded judgments remains poorly understood. We present a human-aligned validation study using the CRaFT framework across Arabic, Bengali, and Spanish, evaluating six judge models, including five open-weight models and GPT-4.1, against paired human annotations across two structurally observable dimensions (Answer Consistency and Explanation Consistency) and three culturally interpretive dimensions (Cultural Fluency, Linguistic Adaptation, and Deviation). Our results reveal a consistent reliability divide: automated judges align substantially better with humans on structural dimensions than on culturally interpretive ones requiring sociocultural reasoning. Reliability further varies across languages, judge architectures, and response-generation models, with several failures reflecting systematic calibration limits rather than prompt underspecification alone. These findings suggest that current automated evaluators are best treated as complementary diagnostic tools rather than replacements for human judgment in culturally sensitive multilingual settings.

title: Ontology-Guided Knowledge Graph Construction from Structured Metadata and Climate Science Publications
abstract: The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. To address this, we introduce an agentic, ontology-guided framework for knowledge graph (KG) construction. Our framework utilizes specialized agents for document understanding, information extraction, ontology conformance, and entity linking. First, an LLM extracts factual knowledge in the form of triples with explicit textual evidence from research papers. Then the triplets undergo a multistage verification process to ground the triplets in the ontology. By enforcing schema constraints and requiring evidence in the form of text fragments, we ensure the data is both semantically consistent and traceable. In an agreement study over 1,000 extracted triplets, Gemini-2.5-flash achieves Cohen's $\kappa$ scores of 0.640--0.700 against three human annotators, matching the human--human agreement range of 0.616--0.689. We applied this framework to 2,000 scientific publications and construct a novel, ontology-grounded KG for climate science with 133,990 nodes and 755,308 relations; of the 23,327 triplets that the publications contribute after validation, 98.96\% are judged correct. The pipeline code and KG is publicly available.

title: Information-Theoretic Design of Sparse Autoencoder-Based Steering
abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based activation steering is a lightweight approach for modifying the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by adding small vectors to hidden states during inference. However, designing effective steering interventions remains challenging. In this work, we develop an information-theoretic framework for analyzing SAE activations through empirical feature-firing distributions. The central object of the framework is the Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) between such firing distributions, which quantifies how far a generated or intervened state deviates from a dataset-induced target distribution. Based on an analytic divergence response for virtually shifted states, we construct steering vectors toward the target firing distribution. The same divergence can also be used to monitor deviation from another empirical distribution, such as a general valid-language distribution. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the steering in a question-mode generation task study. We further use teacher-forced pulse experiments to show that local interventions induce structured downstream JSD responses in later layers, and apply the framework to a safety-related target--contrast response setting for feature analysis.

title: When Does Knowledge Distillation Hurt? Reliability-Aware Distillation for Low-Resource Language Summarization
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a standard approach for compressing sequence-to-sequence models, but its per-sample effects are rarely examined. On the BanSum Bangla summarization benchmark, we find that standard KD improves ROUGE-L by only +0.0003 over a cross-entropy baseline, and that approximately 51.3\% of training samples are estimated to actively harm student validation loss under standard KD. We propose two complementary reliability-aware distillation methods. CHAD (Counterfactual Harm-Aware Distillation) measures per-sample KD usefulness via gradient alignment with the validation loss direction and trains a lightweight gate that generalizes this counterfactual judgment to the full training set. EWAD+CPDP combines token-level entropy-weighted adaptive distillation with a capacity-proportional geometric constraint from a second, vocabulary-incompatible teacher. On BanSum, both methods substantially outperform standard KD: CHAD by +0.0173 ROUGE-L and EWAD+CPDP by +0.0219 ROUGE-L, where standard KD itself improves ROUGE-L by only +0.0003; despite using only 60M parameters, both outperform a fine-tuned Qwen 2.5-3B model (50\texttimes larger). We further evaluate the stronger method, EWAD+CPDP, across 15 typologically diverse XL-Sum languages organised into three sets, beating the CE-only baseline on 10/15 languages; gains are most reliable where the two teachers contribute complementary signal, and weakest where they have saturated or jointly weak target-language coverage. We release code and trained models to support reproducibility and further research on selective distillation.

title: VIDA: A Dataset for Visually Dependent Ambiguity in Multimodal Machine Translation
abstract: Ambiguity resolution is a key challenge in multimodal machine translation (MMT), where models must genuinely leverage visual input to map an ambiguous expression to its intended meaning. Although prior work has proposed disambiguation-oriented benchmarks probing the role of vision, we observe that existing benchmarks remain limited by task-format mismatch, narrow ambiguity coverage, or insufficient visual-dependency validation. Moreover, existing ambiguity evaluations are not well suited to diverse ambiguity types in open-ended translation. To address these limitations, we present VIDA (Visually-Dependent Ambiguity), a dataset of 2,500 carefully curated instances in which resolving an annotated source span requires visual evidence. We further propose Disambiguation-Centric Metrics that use an LLM-as-a-judge classifier to verify whether annotated ambiguous expressions are resolved correctly at the span level. Evaluations with stronger recent LVLMs show that visual disambiguation remains challenging. Using chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning as a diagnostic setting, we observe stronger out-of-distribution disambiguation than with SFT, with robust gains on collective-noun ambiguities and model-dependent gains on sentence-level ambiguities.

title: When Does Concept Erasure Change Behavior?
abstract: Concept erasure can remove linearly recoverable information from a representation without showing that this information influenced the model output being evaluated. For linear edits followed by explicit linear output maps, we characterize the resulting logit change using the output map and representation covariance. We then compare downstream effects with control edits matched for validation-side damage to test whether any benefit depends on the targeted concept. On Bios, Least-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE) reduces gender-probe accuracy to chance but changes only about 0.4\% of occupation-logit energy and yields no detectable improvement in true positive rate (TPR) gaps beyond shuffled-label controls. Iterative Nullspace Projection (INLP) changes more occupation-logit energy at higher ranks, but its small, uncertain fairness gains are accompanied by occupation-accuracy loss. A controlled text shortcut yields a large target-specific gain when the classifier relies on the erased marker. In final-state, next-token audits of TinyLlama and Qwen2.5-7B, gender erasure substantially reduces he/she margins but leaves occupation-token choices intact. These results show that successful erasure, output sensitivity, and downstream benefit are distinct and should be evaluated separately.

title: The Missing ``I Don't Know'': Why Three Reasoning-Reliability Findings Converge on Calibrated Abstention
abstract: Three recent results describe what look like unrelated LLM reliability problems. Yin et al. (2026) show reasoning RL collapses tool-reliability representations. Suleymanov et al. (2026) show that under safety-constrained generation, large models rewrite flagged spans while small models truncate. Bastounis et al. (2024) prove any consistent-reasoning system without an implicit ``I don't know'' function must hallucinate infinitely often on broad problem classes. We argue these findings converge on a single intervention: calibrated abstention is what each independently identifies as the missing capability, even though the unavailability they document, a capability gap, a policy gap, and a recursion-theoretic gap, has a different source in each case. Honesty post-training has narrowed the gap in deployed models, but principled closure of the class Bastounis identifies requires a calibrated abstention function whose training signal at the leaderboard level is absent: dominant benchmarks assign zero reward to decline, so the leaderboard gradient that would select for the function does not exist. We propose four changes to evaluation: triple-scoring, abstention-rate reporting, capability-stratified evaluation, and mandatory calibration metrics. Benchmark reform is necessary, not sufficient, for closing the gap the theorem identifies.

title: CogMem: A Cognitive Memory Architecture for Sustained Multi-Turn Reasoning in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at single-turn reasoning but often lose accuracy and coherence over extended, multi-turn interactions. Recent evaluations such as TurnBench highlight recurring failure modes, including reasoning bias, task drift, hallucination, overconfidence, and memory decay. Current approaches typically append full conversational histories, causing unbounded context growth, higher computational costs, and degraded reasoning efficiency. We introduce CogMem, a cognitively inspired, memory-augmented LLM architecture that supports sustained iterative reasoning through structured, persistent memory. CogMem incorporates three layers: a Long-Term Memory (LTM) that consolidates cross-session reasoning strategies; a Direct Access (DA) memory that maintains session-level notes and retrieves relevant long-term memories; and a Focus of Attention (FoA) mechanism that dynamically reconstructs concise, task-relevant context at each turn. Experiments on TurnBench show that this layered design mitigates reasoning failures, controls context growth, and improves consistency across extended reasoning chains, suggesting that structured hierarchical memory is a promising direction for improving long-horizon multi-turn reasoning in large language models.

title: Language Triggers Hijack Language Circuits: A Mechanistic Analysis of Backdoor Behaviors in Large Language Models
abstract: Backdoor attacks pose significant security risks for Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the internal mechanisms by which triggers operate remain poorly understood. We present the first mechanistic analysis of trigger-induced language-switching backdoors injected during pre-training, studying the Gaperon model family (1B, 8B and 24B). Using activation patching, we localize trigger formation and identify which attention heads process trigger and natural language information. Our central finding is that trigger heads substantially overlap with heads naturally encoding output language across model scales, with Jaccard indices between 0.18 and 0.43 over the top 10 heads identified. This suggests that backdoor triggers do not form new circuits but instead co-opt the model's existing language components and representations. These findings have implications for backdoor defense as detection methods and mitigation strategies could leverage this entanglement between triggers and natural behaviors. More broadly, our work represents a first step toward a more realistic mechanistic understanding of pre-training-injected backdoors in LLMs, paving the way for principled, interpretability-driven defenses.

title: The Guardrail Trinity: Procedural Safety Schemas, Reasoning Chain Decomposition, and Dual-Mode Inference for LLM Guardrails
abstract: Effective LLM safety guardrails must balance adversarial robustness, custom-policy adaptability, and precision on benign prompts with sensitive vocabulary. We introduce the Guardrail Trinity, a data-curation recipe combining procedural safety schemas, reasoning chain decomposition with hard-negative supervision, and a hybrid data blend for fast and slow inference. Experiments across Llama-3.1 and Qwen3 models yield three practical insights. First, strong standard moderation scores can conceal a custom-policy compliance gap; procedural schema variation improves adaptation on our held-out policy-shift probe. Second, augmentation must be matched to model scale and training recipe: smaller models can exhibit training instability, while hard negatives at larger scales can reduce false alarms at a cost to harmful-input recall. Third, hybrid training supports both direct classification and reasoning, with the fast mode retaining strong custom-policy compliance without generating a chain. Together, these findings motivate a deployment playbook that selects data composition, inference mode, and scale jointly, and validates both policy adherence and the trade-off between missed harms and false alarms.

title: Transferable Structural Priors in Continuous Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Continuous diffusion language models struggle with structured generation under hard, variable-length templates. We identify two failure modes: Boundary Attention Drift, in which head-region attention bleeds into padded tails under block-mode training, and Vocab Projection Drift, in which latent-to-token rounding over-projects to low-frequency tokens. The two modes dissociate cleanly across Chinese ci, English sonnets, and E2E NLG: the former is specific to block-mode training, whereas the latter appears in all three datasets regardless of padding regime, isolating padding regime and rounding rule as orthogonal sources of error. To address structural correctness, we adapt constrained decoding to diffusion rounding through a position-template primitive, the $V_i$ rule, instantiated on continuous-diffusion logits as Length-Conditional Voronoi Rounding (LCVR). The same primitive applied to a small autoregressive baseline reaches identical zero-violation rates, showing that structural correctness is delivered by the template, not by the underlying model family. A contribution more readily realised with diffusion backbones is instead cross-domain backbone transfer: initialising a target-domain model from a structurally compatible source-domain backbone yields order-of-magnitude reductions in training steps, while a controlled negative-transfer arm fails to reproduce the speed-up on structural metrics; an attention-span probe localises the transferable component to the source backbone's long-range attention span rather than to its padding regime or corpus size. We further report a calibrated wallclock analysis showing that the dominant cost of diffusion inference is recoverable with standard step-reduction techniques. Together, these results recast several previously scattered structured-generation failures of continuous diffusion as one consistent, transferable, and fixable phenomenon.

title: Auditing Bias Detection Under Source Shift: A Source-Aware Benchmark and Evaluation Protocol
abstract: Bias-detection benchmarks routinely report accuracies above 90\%, but a high number can reflect where a sentence came from as much as whether it contains a stereotype or an unfair claim about a group. We treat this as an evaluation problem and propose an integrated auditing protocol that makes source confounding measurable: an LLM-assisted label audit with cross-family verification, pair-aware splitting with role tracking, source-aware evaluation with a source-only baseline on the actual test split, counterfactual discrimination, and an artifact analysis of edited text. We apply it to a three-source corpus of 10,304 sentences that we audit and release. The audit reduces the global source-only majority baseline from 95.0\% to 55.4\%, and the same protocol shows that the real-only test split still carries a 77.6\% source-only baseline, so confounding is reduced and measured but far from eliminated. Against that baseline, fine-tuned BERT and GPT-2 gain roughly 18 pp and outperform attention-derived models; four augmentation variants that look ordered in the mean fall within seed variance under paired testing; and a real-vs-edited probe separates Gemini counterfactuals from real text, although the signal disappears once the gold label is held fixed and has no measurable accuracy effect. Applied to CrowS-Pairs, the label audit flags 33.2\% of the supposedly neutral members as still containing a group-level stereotype. The main contribution is the protocol, which exposes confounding that standard pipelines would report as results.

title: Code-Switching for Multilingual LLMs
abstract: This tutorial provides a structured overview of code-switching for multilingual large language models (LLMs), connecting linguistic theory, NLP methodology, and human-centered perspectives. Code-switching is a natural communicative practice among multilingual speakers and is increasingly central to LLM interactions, where users bring mixed-language practices to prompts and models themselves may produce mixed-language outputs. The tutorial will cover theoretical foundations from sociolinguistics, code-switching behavior in human-AI interaction, datasets and evaluation benchmarks, synthetic data generation, multilingual LLM training and inference, mechanistic interpretability of unintended language switching, speech and multimodal code-switching, and societal impacts. By synthesizing work across NLP, linguistics, HCI, speech processing, and multilingual communities, the tutorial aims to give participants a coherent view of the field and identify open challenges for building multilingual LLMs that better reflect how multilingual users actually communicate.

title: Post-Deployment Self-Improving Language Agents: Learning, Memory, and Adaptation
abstract: LLM-based systems are increasingly deployed as language agents: long-running NLP systems that retrieve information, call tools, maintain memory, interact with users, and operate in changing environments. After deployment, these systems must contend with evolving user goals, updated knowledge sources, shifting APIs, new tasks, and previously unseen failure modes. Yet adaptation is still often handled through an ad hoc combination of prompt changes, periodic fine-tuning, retrieval updates, memory mechanisms, and manual intervention. The tutorial examines how post-deployment NLP systems can instead be designed as self-improving language agents, drawing on never-ending learning, lifelong learning, continual learning, and recent advances in agentic AI. We take a system-level view of learning: improvement may arise not only from changes to model parameters, but also from persistent changes to memory, knowledge, tools, policies, and other components of the agent and its harness. The tutorial combines literature review with practical running examples (code provided) illustrating different forms of post-deployment learning. We'll examine empirical results and failure cases to understand when adaptation improves a system, when it doesn't, and how such changes can be evaluated. We'll cover a broader transition in NLP: from increasingly capable static models toward developing language systems that can continue to learn and improve responsibly throughout their deployed lifetime.

title: Crayotter: Traceable Multi-Agent Workflows for Long-Form Video Editing
abstract: Long-form video editing over heterogeneous footage requires agents to coordinate source selection, multimodal analysis, timeline construction, narration and subtitle alignment, rendering, and revision while exposing intermediate state for inspection and repair. We present Crayotter, an open-source multimodal multi-agent demo system for prompt-driven long-form video editing. Crayotter organizes production around coverage-aware material preparation, artifact-grounded editing research, and tool-grounded timeline execution. Across these stages, retrieval reports, video analyses, editing blueprints, scheduler events, tool calls, intermediate renders, and final exports are treated as first-class artifacts rather than hidden transient state. The workbench supports local assets, agent-assisted retrieval, progress monitoring, artifact preview, failure diagnosis, interrupted-job resumption, and resource-aware asynchronous execution for long-running workflows. In a 23-theme evaluation, Crayotter achieves the highest human overall score (3.40/5) among the compared systems, with its largest margins in theme alignment, narrative coherence, and editing smoothness. These results show that long-horizon video editing agents can be made traceable, inspectable, and practically controllable through observable production artifacts.

title: NE-Agent: Bringing Agentic AI to Northeast India's Low-Resource Languages
abstract: Northeast India is home to over 220 indigenous languages, yet none are served by existing agentic AI systems. NE-Agent addresses this gap: a terminal-based agentic system that integrates the NE-Stack, a suite of purpose-built language AI components for Northeast India, into a unified conversational pipeline that dynamically selects between retrieval, translation, and transcription tools based on the user's query. The system combines language identification across 11 languages (NE-LID), multilingual dense retrieval (NE-Embed, a LaBSE-based model fine-tuned for 10 Northeast Indian languages), Khasi-to-English translation (fine-tuned NLLB), speech transcription across eight languages (NE-ASR), and generation via a locally-hosted open-source LLM, requiring no API keys or cloud infrastructure. A lightweight LLM-based tool router dispatches each query to the appropriate tool, distinguishing NE-Agent from purely retrieval-augmented systems. NE-Agent is open-source, pip-installable (pip install ne-agent), and ships with a multilingual corpus spanning four languages. To our knowledge, it is the first publicly available agentic system built on indigenous Northeast Indian language AI infrastructure: https://github.com/MWirelabs/ne-agent.

title: Pollux: A Compact Judge and Workflow for Criteria-Based LLM Evaluation
abstract: Evaluating open-ended generation remains non-trivial because quality varies across style, correctness, grounding, and safety. Moreover, a fixed prompt-response abstraction is insufficient for a reusable evaluation system as deployed applications increasingly expose multi-turn dialogues, retrieved evidence, and tool-calling traces. We present Pollux, a universal criteria-based evaluation framework centered on Pollux Judge, a compact Qwen3-4B-based LLM-as-a-Judge that evaluates such heterogeneous interactions through free-form user-defined criteria, scales, and output formats. Pollux follows the criteria methodology represented in the Pollux Benchmark (35 task groups, 2,115 expert-authored prompts), using it as a human-grounded resource for judge validation. The judge is trained with GRPO on Russian- and English-language data and is designed for bilingual deployment through a language-independent interaction schema. On the held-out expert-labeled test set, Pollux reaches a Spearman correlation of 0.744, exceeding every evaluated general-purpose baseline, including models with up to 1.1T parameters, while remaining suitable for local or OpenAI-compatible serving.\par System demonstration video: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1PF6L-RcrS24JVUdaVRi01j237yTdftEd/

title: AI Tour Meeting: Group Travel Planning by LLM Agents
abstract: This paper proposes AI Tour Meeting, a group travel planning framework powered by multiple Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents. The agents are instantiated with distinct personas and collaboratively seek an itinerary that satisfies their constraints and preferences through natural language discussion.\par The framework enables easy and flexible orchestration of such discussions by providing interfaces for configuring agent personas, discussion workflows, monitoring, and LLM deployment. Its primary use case is a simulation tool for analyzing the behavior of multiple LLM agents during tour planning discussions.\par This paper demonstrates the utility of the framework by presenting system validation and several analytical results obtained using the framework.

title: LensLapse: In-Browser Logit Lens for Interactive Exploration of Language Model Training Dynamics
abstract: The logit lens is a standard mechanistic interpretability tool for inspecting a Transformer's predictions across layers. However, existing logit lens tools typically focus on individual checkpoints rather than interactive exploration of a model's training history.\par In this study, we introduce LensLapse, an open-source web application for interactive exploration of a model's training history through token-level interpretability. Users can scrub a slider across public checkpoints from five model families and three multilingual checkpoint suites and observe how per-layer, per-position logit lens predictions evolve from frequency bias to factual knowledge.\par For browser-compatible models, arbitrary user prompts are probed live in the browser via local inference over per-checkpoint model pairs. No server, no API key, no hosting cost, and prompts never leave the user's device.\par Moreover, LensLapse supports local models. A single `pip install` enables users to launch the application and explore their own models and training checkpoints without any additional web setup.\par LensLapse is MIT-licensed and permanently hosted at iamtatsuki05.github.io/lenslapse.\par - GitHub: https://github.com/iamtatsuki05/lenslapse - PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/lenslapse/ - docs: https://iamtatsuki05.github.io/lenslapse/docs/ - YouTube: https://youtu.be/OBnvG9Ru3j8

title: ReqLens: An Interactive Evidence-Grounded Multi-Agent System for Document-to-Requirements Generation
abstract: Large language models can transform project documents into software requirements, but direct generation may introduce unsupported claims and hidden inconsistencies. We present ReqLens, an interactive multi-agent NLP system that extracts candidate requirements from mixed project documents, links them to source evidence, exposes graph-based dependencies and conflicts, and generates a Software Requirements Specification (SRS) through a human-in-the-loop workflow. We evaluate ReqLens on 13 projects using direct-generation and modular baselines, as well as component ablations. ReqLens achieves the strongest overall balance across unsupported-requirement rejection, valid-requirement retention, and seeded-defect filtering. A formative study with four domain experts provided qualitative feedback on the system's interface and review workflow. ReqLens is accompanied by code, data, an installable package, and a narrated screencast.
